From the London Times, July 29. Lord John Russell had to address the House last night under circumstances of unusual difficulty. If he could show that England had not lost credit or weight, that she had not damaged herself by offensive and rejected interference, that , the was still wanted in the settlement of Europe, and could do good, this was so much gain to his hearers and to the public. Although he spoke as the man who þÿ strives some þÿrock vast s weight to þÿthrow, slowly and laboriously, still he left the comforting conviction that there is trouble enough in Italy to render our presence at some future Congress acceptable, if not necessary. Indeed, the innumerable objections to our taking any part in it only end, it would seem, in the thing being unavoidable. The two Emperors have done without us as much as they could ; without us they rushed into war ; without us they made peace ; without us they

unfortunately for them, Italy cannot be settled so easily. The Papal States are taking measures of their own ; Tuscany, Modena, and Parma have thrown off their rulers, and both France and Austria disclaim all intention of employing their soldiers to bring back the old state of things. There would seem, then, little prospect of France and Austria settling Italy by themselves. The Peace of Villafranca binds none but themselves, and only obtains for each certain term6 from the other. It docs not bind Italy. It docs not bind Europe. It can only pledge the two Emperors to further the proposed Italian Confederation. If they

to reduco to terms the rough notes of their hasty peace, they must cither confess all they have done for Italy to be utterly abortive, or they must, at the eleventh hour, invoke other j operated with France up to this very day in Powers to contribute their counsel and their sanction. The embarrassment, therefore, the rash interference, the meddling without settled purpose, al) usually charged to England, are this time chargeable entirely on the Continental belligcreuts ; and it is their fault þÿ not ours that at this moment Italy lies, onu may say, in the gutter, as the Imperial Crown did now and then ; and the Italians are likely to fight it out among themselves. If, then, there is anything discreditable aud perplexing in the present state f things, the reproach aud the helplessness belong entirely to France and Austria, not to ourselves. All that England is answerable for is her own interference, which, as it was ineffective, so may be considered harmless. The general effect of our counsels was to represent to Franco that if she pushed her successes too far she might find herself in collision with all the nentral Powers, and so involved in a war of uncertain consequences ; and to Austria, on thb other baud, that, as the neutral Powers would not interfere to establish her dominion South of the Alps, she must attempt it at her own risk. No doubt, this has touched the pride of both oorabatants ; but, both allege that they have made hasty as a peace in consequence of these unfriendly and
threatening communications, it cannot be said that the neutral Powers have done harm, or done nothing at all Lord Palmerston gives, as wo trust, the right versioa of a current tale,

$ T « © 1 Q) D I A >11 S « that England had heedlessly put it in the power j uf Napoleon III. to show to Francis Joseph the hard terms we were ready to recommend him. H siys wo have simply performed the friendly office of communicating to Austria the terms on which France would make peace. However, all tli is will be cleated by time ; aud we trust the F vign Secretary will come out of it bet- i ter 'ban i.v Envoy Extraordinary to Vienna. What the Peace of Villalranca happily did is one thing; what it hupp ly, or unhappily, could not do, is another. It could transfer a province from one Emperor to another, and enable them to consign it to a third Power. It could place another province in a somewhat new political position, to receive its character front the will of the two contracting Powers It could also pledge them both to further a certain speculative proposal. That the two Emperors should cease to lead their subjects to mutual slaughter on those conditions was their own affair, and a most happy event for the world. The Peace of Villafranca could not and did not give Princes, Constitutions, Federations, Presidencies, and what not, to the other States of Italy, neither represented at Villafranca nor at the di-posul of the two Emperors. These two latter will seud their Plenipotentiaries to Zurich to put the terms of peace into form, but neither they, it seems, nor anybody else, dream of the affairs if all Italy, being so easily disposed of. No doubt, France and Austria will do as much as they can for this purpose. They are, how-

ever, fully aware of the impossibility of doing all they could wish ; and Count Walewski iufirms the British Ministers that his Government has always desired and still desires to see the great Powers concur for the definitive settlement of Italy. Accordingly, France hopes that the Powers will be able to meet to confer on all the questions raised by the actual state of things in Italy, and which are connected with the geueral interest. The precise meaning of these terms is not a matter ot importance. They are I an admission that the Peace of Villafranca has done nothing really but transfer Lombardy to Sardinia, aud promised something else, which is to receive its interpretation from time. The would, if possible, settle Italy, or divide it. But, I arr ingemeiit which it is competent for Austria and Frinco to make, as regards the territory at their dispo-al, iiid whatever else they can do, may he don very shortly indeed. It will constitute part of what is called þÿ the actual state of things in þÿItaly, and of course it will bo necessary that tee Powers invited to confer upon that state of things should know all about the terms of peace. Then comes the further business, which may he undertaken this year or the next, by five Powers or by more þÿ viz., the soitlemeut of Italy. Of course, if there is to be a Congress for this purpose, England will be only too true to her unbroken prescription if she have a voice in meet, then, by their representatives at Zurich, ; it. We h.tvc repeatedly interfered in the af-
fairs of Italy at the invitation of various Powers, aud it is neellesi now to demonstrate our right to do so if we are so minded. We have co-

sugge-tiuns to the Court of Naples; and, when L .rd Clarendon at the Congress of Paris called aitcution to the siate of the Peninsula, he only did what he had a perfect right to do at a very proper occasion. If anything is done lor Italy þÿ it is for the interest of Europe that the concurrence of every Power should be secured. It is said, indeed, that the Emperor of Austria strongly objected to a Conlerenee. No doubt he has reasons, and they are the very reasons why any Conference would be incomplete without his representative. This, however, is a matter for mature deliberation. As Lord John Russell says, a Confederation may be a good and wise measure, but impossible this year or the next. The general settlement of Italy, therefore, is not likely to be despatched as quickly as the conveyance of Lombardy. It will be a work of time, and, as far as we can see, the Emperors of France and Austria will be very glau to leave England and the other Powers at liberty to carry out their own views of Italian regeneration. We trust that we shall consider long before we undertake to interfere.

The Peace and Italy When the monk Varnes among other emissaries of the Clerical Power was sent from Rome to Paris, in 1849, to secure the aid of the French Republic in restoring the clerical authority in the Eternal City, he went about retailing a story of Pope Gregory XVI. and

the Prince Louis Napoleon Bonaparte, which the peace just concluded in Europe is likely enough to revive. Gregory XVI. ruled or misruled the Romagna when the sons of Hortense fleshed their maiden swords in revolt against the Papacy. The brother of Louis Napoleon, as is well known, died in the couise of that revolutionary outburst, and, as Varnes told his tale, Pope Gregory pardoned the remaining Prince with the words, þÿ My benediction shall descend upon this young Napoleon, and he shall live and render immense service to the þÿChurch. The Holy Father's holier successor, Pio IX , doubtless held the prophecy fulfilled ten years ago, when he came riding in state into silent and sullen Rome, and passed from the superb square of St. John Latcrau beneath the frowning shadow of the Coliseum to his Te Deum at St. þÿPeter sbetween two lines of French soldiery commissioned to protect him by the Prince- President Napoleon. Will lie now regard the mystic speech of his predecessor as more completely crowned with meaning by his appointment to preside over the affairs of the great Italian Confederation which the same Napoleon, now Emperor and Conqueror, has summoned into being ? For a just reply to this question we must await, of course, the arrival of full details from Europe of the steps which led to the creatiou of the new Confederacy, and of the nature of the authority by which its affairs are to be administered. The New Mexican Treaty From a Washington correspondent, who possesses tin; happy faculty of being able tu penetrate the logs in which tbe devotees of wax and red tape envelope themselves, we receive a synopsis of Mr. þÿMeLaue s now Convention with the Liberal Government of Mexico. The moderation of the concessions obtained is creditable to the Envoy. There is no acquisition of territory. Rights of way authorizing our adventurous vanguard to push into Mexico in pretty much any direction they may please to select ; to cross the Southern States at Tehuantepec, aud the Northern States from the tortuous Rio Grande to the puarl-paven waters of the Gulf of California ; to land their wares at the ports ol Sonora duty free, aud to transport them without toll and in safety to Arizona ; protection, armed if necessary, and by American troops if no others can be had, to the several lines of transit ; and the liberty of unrestricted and unquestioned worship of God, such are a few of the advantages which the

$ ® t u ® x v? c negotiations of our Minister have secured. But this project of a treaty contains within it the germ of another still more valuable. The Mexican Government expresses its readiness to execute a treaty of alliance with the United States, so strict and intimate as to amount to a protectorate to be wielded by the latter over tbe domestic affairs of its di-tructed neighbor. Of the precise limitations of this proffered power we have no information. It is evidently a proposition of grave importance ; one in the presence of which any Administration, however courageous, might fairly hesitate ; and from which, therefore, we apprehend, the actual Cabinet of Mr. Buchanan will shrink in terror. The present is, nevertheless, the grandest | opportunity ever offered to this Government for solving the most difficult question of its external politics. The treatment aud fate of Mexico have been the circle which the most ingenious of American statesmen have endeavored vainly to square. Up to this very moment thoughtful men are puzzling themselves with conjectures as to the mode in which, and the eventual time when, the Mexican problem may be expected to be solved. The opportunity tor its solution is now suddenly sprung upon us. It is possible for Mr. Buþÿchanan sAdministration to secure to Mexico a prosperous future ; and to remove all difficulties in the way of her peaceful absorption into the Union, when the proper period shall have arrived for her þÿ manifest þÿde.-iiny tube fulfilled. It is, perhaps, too mu. h to hope for

any decisive steps from the timid and temporizing powers that now be at Washington ; but the well-informed will watch the immediate course of the Government on this question with intense curiosity. þÿ - Ibid. ' Special Dispatch to the New-York Times.

Washington, Monday, July 25. The draught of a Treaty just scut hither by Hon Robert Me Lane to be submitted to our Government, contains provisions of tiie very highest importance to this country. 1 am fortunately enabled to furnish you with a summary of its more striking stipulations: which areas follows : 1. Rights of way across the Northern States, between the Rio Grande and ports ou the Gulf of California, with guarantees for their protection and safety. 2 Rights of way, and valuable privileges of transit, secured to the American Company holding the lsihmus of Tehuantepec. 3 The privilege of erecting and maintaining warehouses at the termini of the several Transit Routes. 4 The right of transporting troops and munitions over such routes, and to send troops to protect them in default of Mexico fulfilling that duty. 5. Free entry and transit of goods belonging or consigned to American citizens in Arizona, through the ports of the Gulf of California, aud across Sonora. 6 Entire and unquestionable freedom of religious opinion, and religious worship throughout the Republic. 7. A clause indicating the willingness ol the Mexican Government to accept a modified form of Protectorate at the hands of the United States; in other words to solemnize another Treaty, inform one of alliance, offensive and defensive, but in substance creating a Protcotorate, whenever the United States shall signify its willingness to enter into such engagements. What is granted, and what is offered by this

Convention, is all that the American people can desire, or could properly assume ; and it only remains to be seen whether Mr. Buchanan will have the pluck to approve the work of his Envoy, and make the Americanization of Mexico the crowning historical lact of his Administration.

NEUTRAL RIGHTS. The Herald publishes the following : þÿ The important State Taper as to the position of the United States upon the question of neutral rights has been completed, and was dispatched to all our Ministers in Europe by the Persia on Wednesday. It will create a most profound impression, and demonstrate that the present Administration will maintain the dignity, character, and moral position uf the United States. As one of the first commercial nations of the earth, we can no longer permit the grave questions which may arise affecting commerce to be disposed of without our voice aud influence

þÿ The present manifesto lays down broad principles which will govern us in the maintenance of our rights as neutrals, and there is every reason to believe that the position now assumed will bo adopted by all the great nations of Europe. The principal points are, of course, with reference to a limitation of articles which shall be deemed contraband of war. Tba United States holds that nothing should be embraced in this list but the direct aud immediate munitions of warfare, sucli as powder, muskets, cannon, lead, aud saltpetre, etc. Coal, which is the very foundation of manufacturing and commercial transactions, is declared by the United States not to be contraband of war, and any attempt to construe it otherwise will bo viewed as an eucronchmeut upon our commerce. So, also, are breadstuffs not contraband of war. The broad doetiine is also reiterated that a free flag covers the cargo. þÿ While the dispatch makes uo allusion to privateering, it is well understood as a settled principle of the American doctrine that uuder no circumstances will we abandon that right. THE PRESS IN RUSSIA. Among the various measures of internal reform recently instituted in the Russian Empire, the enfranchisement of the Press is that which, next to the emancipation of the serfs, will naturally be regarded with the greatest interest in this country. Newspapers are now the recognized organs of international intercourse. With all our travelling and all our trade, it is still, comparatively speaking, but a small portion of the population which can visit foreign States, and learn the customs and opinions of their inhabitants from actual survey. By the great majority of the people this species of information can only be acquired through the Newspaper-Press þÿ through those publications in which a nation speaks aloud, and in which it presents a reflection of its own sentiments and manners.

We have more than once during the last few months given extracts from the Russian papers, by which the tone of opinion in that empire might be to some extent appreciated, nor can we deny that the freedom of discussion there exhibited was quite ns great as the ciieumstancc would have led us to expect. It appears, however, that the Russian Government has experienced that peculiar embarrassment which is all but inseparable fiorn any censorship of the Press, however liberally exercised. It is known, of course, that newspapers in Russia are not absolutely free to publish what they choose. Their contents are subjected to revi-iou by certain authorities, and, as a natural consequence, it is assumed abroad that what those authorities thus permit to appear they must positively approve. In other words, the opinions of a Russian journal are held and taken to be those also of the Russian Government, inasmuch as the officers of Government having exercised a preliminary censorship could have stopped without difficulty the publication of any matter deemed objectionable. To counteract the impressions thus naturally disseminated, the Journal de St. Petersbourg has just published an article professing to describe authoritatively the relations actually subsisting betweeu the Government and the Press. In these observations we are told that the assumed connexion has no existence whatever, and that, in reality, the Government of Russia when enfranchising the Press expressly intended to withdraw in a proportionate degree its own

responsibility. It still professes to exercise a supervision, but only for general purposes of morality, religion, and order. That kind of duty it cannot abdicate ; but, with that single reservation, Russian journals are permitted to publish what they please, aud their opinions, tbeicfore, must be taken as the opinions of tlieir conductors, and not as those of the Government. i Provided only that the preliminary conditions of propriety are satisfitd, the censors inquire no further. All beyond this is the work of the journal itself, for which it is accountable in the ordinary way to its customers and the public. We believe this statement to be fairly and j case, no doubt, hut it is one from which, under truly made. There is a difficulty about the the circumstances, it was hardly possible to escape. Liberty in the case of the Press, as in that of the individual, must he distinguished from licence ; nor docs freedom cf discussion imply any privilege of doing wrong. It is perfectly true, as the Ilussim Government assumes, that the Press should he prevented from out raging principles hold in universal respect ; but it is also true that in a well-oigallizi d commonwealth the restrictions necessary for this purpose would be furnished by opinion itself. We in England have also laws controling the action of the Press, hut it is (baud in practice that they may be left unnoticed, and that the true corrective lies in the good sense of the public. The prosecution of a journal for sedition or blasphe-

my, or any of the offences which the Russian censorship is intended to prevent, is a tiling unheard of among us, and for the best of all leasons. The voice of the people is far stronger than that of the Attorney-General, and it speaks in his place. A newspaper offending against public decency would not survive its offence. It would have no tenders ; and, being thus destitute of any mischievous power, it might be left to expire. In the infancy, however, of a free Press, and in a country hut imperfectly civilized, it might be reasonable doubted whether such correctives would he at once forthcoming, nor can we blame the Rus-iau Government tor presuming that its surveillance may he required lor some time longer. It will always, however, remain impossible to separate authority from responsibility in these matters of the Tress. When the Russiau Government admits, as it docs in the article before us, that it undertakes to revise and sanction the contents of a newspaper, foreign readers will always hold it more or less answerable for the opiuions conveyed. If, for instance, any remarks were to appenr in a Russian journal strongly condemnatory of England or her policy, we should feel ourselves unable to accept such observations as the reflection of private or even publio opinion only, for we should be aware that the production, if not suggested by authority, had been at any rate þÿ examined and þÿapproved. took to prohibit anything contrary to the con- Knowing that the Russian þÿ Government under-

aideration due to Sovereigns and þÿGovernments, we should naturally feel that, it the supposed trade bad not been prohibited, the consideration in which tl»e censors held us must be very low. The opinions might not be actually or directly those of the authorities themselves, but they would, at all events, be such as the authorities, after preliminary scrutiny, and with full power in their hands, would not be at the trouble of suppressing. There is another point, too, deserving of consideration At the present day we are witnessing the formation of a public opinion more comprehensive and powerful than has ever yet been seen þÿ an opinion proceeding not from one country alone, but from all civilized countries together. The opinion of Europe, it is hoped, will act as a check upon even absolute Governments, þÿ will maintain the principles of peace, and oppose the doctrines of war, þÿ will gradually diffuse good maxims of government, and promote the happiness of mankind. What this power, in short, has done for particular countries, it will now in its aggregate force do for Christendom. We hail with gratification any fresh contributor to so desirable a consummation, and tender all our sympathies to the Press of Russia ; but, if that Press is really to exercise its proper influence, it must acquire its full liberty and independence. We want to hear the people of Russia speak. At present we bear them only through certain modifications of tone. We obtaiu their opinions, but only after correction and

revision, so that we can never be quite sure of our inferences. Perhaps, out of the þÿ consideration due to the British þÿGovernment, some wholesome reflections on our policy may have been suppressed ; or, out of the considciation due to auother Government, some welcome approval of our the bidden to see proceedings may have been for- light. The veiy knowledge of this contingency checks our conclusions, aud the influence of the Russian Press is so far impaired. It is . tii prising to observe that this selfevident principle lias sometimes been overlooked at home. Not long ago certain eminent politicians expressed their desire that the English Piess should cither pass altogether without comment the acts of the French Government, or speak of them with the same kind of reserve as would he observed in France itself. In the very same breath, however, they acknowledged their conviction that the French Government was peculiarly open to impression from English opinion, and that the influence exercised by this opiuiun was beneficial. I hero is no question, we believe, about this fact, and it is simply a proof of the þÿEmperor s sagacity. But what weight would Napoleon III. attach to English opiuion if lie got of from the breasts the people, but disguised lor it, not in its purity and truth the put pose ol suiting his assumed desires? Take away the freedom ol expression aud the whole value of the thing is lost. The Emperor of the French likes to know what the people of England really and the he the last man in actually think, aud he would world to wish that valu-

able information should roach him in a corrupt or imperfect form. It is not, however, in any spirit of cavil or reproach that we make these remarks upon Russian journalism. Perhaps it was uot to be expected that a Goverumeut which was recently one of the most despotic in the world should proclaim on a suddeu the the Press. Wo take the absolute freedom of improvement as we find it, and with all satisfaction. It is evident that Russia contains writers of ability, and that its journals, if they proceed as they bavo begun, will soon obtain a good position iu the eyes of Europe. We are inlurtucd, too, aud we cuu readily believe, that newspaper leudois are fouud in great numbers even iu the rural districts; that they multiply rapidly, and that questions likely to touch the passions of the are such as that of serf enfranchisement, multitude, discussed without violence or disorder. It is said, in short, that the freedom of the Press already exists at St. Petersburg more truly than at Vienna, and so very substantial a reform ought to be cordially hailed by all lovers of liberty in Europe. þÿ London Times,

The Motives on which (his draft is based, are, as follows : Agreeable to the Rcsciipt of 9th December 1825 3, cfr. the Ordinance of the 7 h February 1823 8 and the Rescript of the 6th February 1849, summonses issued, in accordance with a Royal license, to obtain an annulment by judicial act of bonds lost in the Danish Westindia Pos-essions, are to be published in the Berling political and advertising gazette, and in the St. Croix Avis. The same is applicable with regard to notices to creditors, as the enactments emanated with regard to these latter do not pr scribe any publication in tho St. 1 liotn® Tidcudo. How inadequate this is, owing to the small circulation c.ich of these newspapers enjoy out of the island in which it is published, has long been admitted, and as the extending to the Colonics of the law of the 30th November 1857, concerning proclatnata issued under the partition of estates, has afforded au oppo: tunity to make a change iu this respect with regard to notices to creditors, it has been considered right to endeavor, at the same time, to make a similar change with regard to publications of summonses in suits for annulment. There has also been found reason to take under consideration whether, on this occasion, a change ought not to be introduced with regard to the enactment in the Rescript of the 9th December 1825 3, that all suits for annulment in the Danish Westindia Islands am to be pleaded in the Westindia Uppereourt. cember 1788 the cases of annulment of lost Westindia mortgage bonds, treated of in tho 5, 6, 7 and 8, tveie to be sued for þÿ in the Court of the jut Udiction iu which the mortgaged property was þÿsituated, by which, according to the Oidinance of the 3 1 t March 1755 3 and 4, was to he understood the court of first instance under the jurisdiction of which the mortgaged property was situated, as the Rescript of the 25th January 1776 had, only as far as recording was concerned, placed estates under the Uppereourt, (cfr. the Royal License of the 7th December 1804, treated of iu the Jur. In the report laid before the Royal Chancery by

the former Westindia Government concerning the extension of the law to the Colonies, the reason given for referring annulment-suits to | the Uppercourt was, that it was considered advisable, þÿ to lessen the delay creditors often must þÿsuffer. COMMUNICATION. To the Editor of the Avis. Sir, The election that was held at St. Thomas on the 8th inst. gives rise to questions of an interesting and highly important naturj. First, contrary to all precedent, and, I am sorry to add, in neglect of the courtesy due to a numerous and important class of citizens, the day for the election was fixed not only on the Sabbath-day of the Israelites, but on one of their greatest holydays in the year, thus making it impossible for them to attend at the elections, which I ain positively assured on the best authority that they would otherwise have done. It is to be hoped, therefore, that at future elections, the Government will take cognizance of this, and fix a day on which all creeds can attend without religious scruples. But there is another circumstance connected with the same election, which renders that election null and void. One viUer only met, and elected six members to the Colonial Council, but it does not appear that the superintendant of the Poll and hia two assistants gave their votes at all. Now, according to ( 18 of the Colonial law, þÿ when no more persons offer to vote, then the superintendant and the assistants enter their own þÿvotes, thus making it incumbent on these three persons to vote if any one else has previously voted. If no one has voted, then the superintendant &c. need not vote, but, if any, if only one, has voted, then they shall give their votes It is obvious, that three additional votes may entirely alter the result of the elec-

tion, either by giving the elected persons more than one vote, or by falling on persons, who, in consideration of existing circumstances will deem themselves fairly elected, and accept the membership. Now, tliis omission, if it really has taken place, entirely invalidates the election for St. Thomas, and the consequence thereof is, that no Colonial Council can be legally held, or, if held, can legally deliberate or advise or decide upon any matter soever, before a now election in strict conformity to the law has been held at St. Thomas. Without this, all and every Act of the Council will be null and void. And, even should report have been incorrect about this omission, 1 deem it in fairness necessary, that a .lew election should bo held at St. Thomas; for, in in/ humble opinion, as there exist in our Colonies no legal differences in the social or political rights of the different religious creeds, the Government has no more a right to fix on a Saturday than on a Sunday for holding elections. St. Croix, 13th Oct. 1859. Heilbutii.

CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX. FRIDAY, 14th OCTOBER, 1859. The public of St. Thomas remain still firm to their intcution not to return members to the Colonial Council, under its present cumbrous and useless constitution. At the election held on Saturday last, one solitary voter recorded his vote. The St Thomas Times considers it unnecessary to make known the names of the gentlemen upon whom this individual bestowed his choice, as none of them, in the opinion of that paper, would bo willing to respond to such a nomination That the Important colony of St. Thomas should remain unrepresented in the Colonial Council, is a circumstance of too much weight to remain unnoticed by the Government in Denmark. We are happy to see that so much public spirit prevails in one of the Danish Westindia Colonies, as clearly to show how the Colonial Council is valued by those whom it was intended to benefit. We, at the same time, regret that self-interest, reigning, as it does, supreme over every other in this community, should yet be so powerful as to stifle tho utterance of the real opinions of its members in respect to the value which is here set on that institution.

The London Papers to tho 3rd inst. contain no news of great importance, if we except the return of Capt. þÿM Clintoek and his gallant crew from their successful search for the relics of Sir John Franklin and his comrades Tho following most interesting letter has been forwarded by the Secretary ol the Admiralty for publication : þÿ

Yacht Fox, R. Y. S. Sir, þÿ I beg you will inform the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty of the safe return to this country of Lady þÿFranklin f s inal searching expedition, which I have had the honour to conduct. Their lordships will rejoice to hear that our endeavours to ascertain the fate of the þÿ Franklin þÿExpedition have met with complete success. At Point Victory, upon the N.W. coast of King þÿWilliam Island, s a record has been found, dated April 25, 1848, and signed by Captains

ed that her þÿMajesty ships s Erebus and Terror were abandoned on April 22, 1848, in the ice, five leagues to the N.N.W., and that the survivors, in all amounting to 106 souls, under the command of Captain Crozier, were proceeding to the Great Fish river. Sir John Franklin had died on June 11, 1847. Many deeply interesting relics of our lost contrymen have been picked up on the western shore of King þÿWilliam s Island, and others obtained from the Esquimaux, by whom we were informed that (subsequent to their abandonment) one ship was crushed and sunk by the ice, and the other forced on shore, where she has ever since remained, affording them an almost inexhaustible mine of wealth. Being unable to penetrate beyond Bellot Straits, the Fox wintered at Brentford Bay, and the search þÿ including the estuary of the Great Fish River, and the discovery of 800 miles of coast line, by which we have united the explorations of the former searching expeditions, to the north and west of our position, with those of James Ross, Dease, and Simpson, and Rae to the south þÿ has been performed by sledge journeys this spring, conducted by Lieutenant Hobson, R.N., Captain Allen Young, and myself. As a somewhat detailed report of our proceedings will doubtless be interesting to their lordships, it is herewith enclosed, together with a chart of our discoveries and explorations ; and at the earliest opportunity I will present myself at the Admiralty to afford further information, and lay before their lordships the record found

at Point Victory. þÿ I have the honour, (Signed) F. L. þÿM Clintock, Captain R N. To the Secretary of the Admiralty. It also states, on good authority, that the treaty will he a fulfilment of the preliminaries of Villafranca. Other questions arising out of the settlement of the affairs of Italy will be referred to a superior jurisdiction, by which it is evidently meaDt that a Congress will be held. The Paris Presse contains a remarkably interesting letter, giving a detailed account of the recently discovered conspiracy at Constantinople. The correspondent says that the Turkish Governmeut has taken extraordinary precautions to conceal the real character of the plot. A vast secret society, consisting of not less than 15,000 or 18,000 members, among whom were many Pachas and men of the highest rank in Turkey, had determined to arrest the Sultan and his Ministers and change the form of Government. The leaders of the conspiracy were the Sheik Ahmed, a Kurdc; a distinguished general officer named Toherkep ; Hussein Pacha, who served at tho siege of Kars ; Hassan Pacha, a General of artillery ; Djafer Pacha, an Albanian ; and the mufti of the couucil of Tephane, Bckir- Effcndi Hassan Pacha, doubly a traitor, betrayed the conspirators to Riza Pacha, the minister at war. It is reported that he was led to take this step by a resolution voted by a majority that in case of resistance the Sultan and all his

ministers should be put to death. It is, however, very generally believed that this story is an invention of Hassan Pacha's to excuse himself. Arif Effendi, a functionary of some importance, who was one of the conspirators, endeavoured, it is said, to dissuade Hassan Pacha from his projeot of betrayal, but finding his eloquence unavailing, he joined in tho denunciation and made a full confession. Djafer Pacha, while beiDg escorted in a boat with 10 others, on their way to prison, eluded the vigilance of his guards, jumped into the water, and has not since been heard of. As he was a good swimmer it is thought possible that he may have escaped. There are various versions as to the designs of the conspirators if they had been successful. Some say that they intended to proclaim the

þÿSultan brother, s others his eldest son. A draft of a circular dispatch to the Powers of Europe has been found, in which it is declared that there was uothingin the revolution hostile to progress, civilisation, or, most especially, to Christiaus. The prisoners who have been examined have for the most part openly avowed the facts with which they are charged. One, a Circassian, spoke with such violence that he was summarily condemned to death. The Sultan has refused to confirm the sentence. It is said that the Sultan means to attend a sitting of the court of inquiry, being curious to hear some of the leading conspirators state their grievances.

Presenting such a summons, shall not be sufficient, in conformity with the Danish þÿCode s 1-24-54, to stay the execution of the sentence appealed, for a longer time, than six months reckoned from the expiration of the term of execution fixed in the sentence, unless there be presented a certificate from the þÿSecretary Of- s fice of the Supreme-Courts, of the summons having been delivered there with due attestation of its having been served. Such certificate shall be given in the Secreþÿtary Office s of the Supreme-Court in duplicate, for the same fee, as for a single certificate. 3. With regard to such summonses to the Supreme-Court as have been taken out before the recording of this law in the Courts ol the Westindics, the enactment in 2 shall not come in force before the expiration of 6 months alter

the recording has been effected. The Motives on which the above draft is based, are, as follows : In the Royal Rescript of the 13th October 1758, by which the Governor-General of the Danish Westindia Islands was authorized to issue summouses and counter-summonses to the Supreme-Court in suits from the Westindies, it is enacted, that the summons thus given is to be delivered to the person having demanded the same, and on whom it is incumbent, immediately, or as soon as possible, to have the writ served, and thereafter to send the original writ with an attestation of its having been served, as well as a copy of the same, to the Danish Chancery, where the original writ was to he furnished with the requisite stamppaper, and recuivo an attestation of having been presented there, and be confirmed under the R iyal seal, without which attestation no summons was to bo accepted in the Supreme-Court ; this enactment has, with the modifications introduced by the Placard of the 21st May 1800 and the Royal Resolution of 19th February 1850, been repealed in the Royal Resolution ot tin 14th May 1850 (Departments Tidende Ibr 150, pages 1331-l335j, it being requisite, that sum-

ft T\ ft ft. ft r: x 1 1 (i ft « mouses issued here in the name of the Supr, me- Court and signed by the Governor and having the Governments seal aitached, should, as formerly, after being duly served, be forwarded to the þÿSecretary s Office of the Supreme-Court to be furnished with the necessary stamppaper and have the seal of the Supreme-Court duly attached. The object in authorising the Governor lo issue summonses to the Supreme-Court, is, as stated iu the Rescript of the 13th October 1758, that suits appealed to the Supreme-Court, may, the sooner, bo brought to a close and the time sav d which would otherwise be required to send the summons backwards and forwards to have it served on the parties concerned ; but, nevertheless, the enactment iu the Rescript may be applied by the party who takes out such a summons in a manner, that would retard the filial decision of the ease, and oblige the adverse party to take out a counter-summons to the Supreme-Court, merely for the purpose of obtaining a final decision iu the suit. The appellant may, namt ly, make use of the summons to the Supreme-Court, issued by the Government, to stay the execution of the sentence passed by the Uppercourt, and have the summons served on all the parties concerned in these islands, but omit theicaftcr to forward it to the þÿSecretary O s ffice of the Supreme-Court. As the suit, thus, cannot, as is the case in suits in which the summons to the Supreme- Court lias been taken out in the þÿSecretary s Office of the Court, b put on the annual Order

of the Court, nor, as an anticipated suit, on the older of tho day, tire appellant is not exposed to receive a sentence for non-appearance, and even if the appellee has retained a lawyer in the Supreme Court and placed the documents of the case in his hands and a copy of the writ of summons served, that his interest may bo properly looked after, yet, the case cannot be brought before the court, although the appellee, according to the Danish þÿCode s 1-4-33 ought to have his costs refunded him by the nonappearing appellant, the latter being besides fined by tlm Court, according to the existing rules for such eases, for frivolous and vexatious litigation. This difficulty may certainly be avoided by taking out a counter-summons, which, iu consequence, is frequently done here by the appellee ; but in all such oases in which the latter had no particular reason to appeal the scuteuce of the Uppercourt, additional expcn.-cs are entailed upon him, particularly, if the case is of such a nature, that he might altogether have omitted to appear before the Suprem -Court. This drawback was, as may be seen from the collection of Law-opinions of Privy-Couusel or St unpe IV Vol, Pages 659-662, already rem i ked a few years after the Rescript of the 13tli Octoh t 1758 was published, ami according to the rein irks there, it might bo supposed, that a Royal Rescript of 13th October 1765 bad removed this drawback by enacting, that the Governor-General was to forward to ihe R iyal Chance, ry, by every vessel leaving the

islitid for Denmark, certified copies of all writs of summons s to the Supreme-Court taken out here , and that the cases should then immediately bo put on the Order of the Supremo- Court, which Rescript is also quoted in Bangs and Larsens process V Vol. p. 577; but such a Rescript was, as modern investigations have pioved, never issued, and the remark in tho collection of þÿStampe sopiuious 1. c. with regard to it, originates probably iu a mistake on the pa t of the editor, ct'r. the preface to Vol 1st. On account of the enactments existing at present with regard to the appeal of Westindia cases to the Supremo-Court, the enactment thought of in 1765 will uot be sufficient to remove the drawback tieated of ; for, as Westindia suits, agreeable to the Ordinance of tho 29th May 1807 1, cau only be brought before the Supiemo-Oourt 6 months after the summons has been duty s rved, the time for a case coming befoie the court could never be appointed agreeable to a copy of tho summons forwarded by Government, which did not show that the sommous had been served ; it being necessary to await the arrival of a summons provid d with an attestation of its having been duly s rved. The qa stion, as to how the said drawback could t moved, huvi.ig been under the consider ili ne Ministry of Justice and tho 1 Supreme-Court, as well as the Westindia Uppercourt, tho Minister of Finances has request-

ed the Government to lay before the Colonial Council a draft of a law, enacting, in accordance with the opinions given on the subject, that the presentation of an appeal-summons to the Supreme-Court shall not stay the execution of a sentence of the Westindia Uppercourt in any civil case longer than 6 months from the expiration of tho terminus executions fixed ill the sentence of the Uppercourt, unless a certificate from t lie þÿSecretary s Office of the Supreme- Court be produced, to tho effect, that the summons has been delivered there with due attestation of its having been served ; and to prevent tile 1 iss an app. Hunt might be subjected to by the summons to the Supreme-Court, or of the certificate given in the þÿSecretary s Office of said C mit, being lost on its way, summonsis to the Supreme-Court, as well as the certificates in question, shall be issued in duplicate, with- I out any enhancement of the fee, so that the different copies may be forwarded by diffeicnt posts. To the different paragraphs of the above draft the following remaiks are offered: ad 1. This enactment comprises not only summonses to the Supreme-Court in civil cases appealed from the Uppercourt, but, in the same manner as the Royal Resolution of 14th May 1850, also those cases which, notwithstanding the Placard of the 10th April 1844, may yet, agreeable to tli e Danish þÿCode s 1-6-19 and the Ordinance of the 25th May 1804 13, be appealed from the lower-courts here directly to the Supreme-
Court.

ad 2. The term of 6 months fixed will be quite sufficient for the appellant, who, to stay the execution, must have taken out a summons before the expiration of the terminus cxecutionis, þÿ to have the same served not only on all parties concerned in the Danish Westindia Possessions, hut in case of the party in whose favor tho sentence has been given being in tho Mothercountry, also on him, there, and thereafter to have a certificate from the þÿSecretary O s ffice of the Supreme-Court sent out here. Should the party in whose favor the sentence has been given, be in foreign parts, he will umst 1 kely have an attorney in these islands, or in the Motherconntry, or there will be some person here, on whom the summons, iu accordance with the ptinciples laid down in the Danish þÿCode 1-4-13, s 5-10-3, and the Placard of the 30th November 1821, may be served in his stead, and under all circumstances it must be possible to serve the summons in the manner enacted by the Danish þÿCode s 1-4-10 and 12, on the person who, according to the Code's 1- 12-23, had been bis attorney in the case appealed. It is therefore not probable that an appellant should ever he able to plead, as an excuse, the impossibility of having the summons duly served ; an impossibility which, it it were to be proved in any ease, would, in accordance with the principles of the Rescript of tho 15th August 1806 (efr. þÿBang s and þÿLarsen s process, 252, 3id V. page 460,) be sufficient to postpone tli e execution of the sentence ap-

pealed, beyond the time fixed. The Danish þÿCode 1 s -24-54 lias been quoted in the Draft, for the purpose of denoting, that no change is to take place in the special enactments of the D. C. 1-6-23, tho Ordinance of the 13th January 1792, the 18th May 1825 72 and others By þÿ duo þÿattestation of the serving of the summons, is meant, that the summons must be provided wilh such an attestation, that the case, in accordance with the Ordinance of 29th May 1807, can lie appointed for being pleaded in the .Supreme-Court, at the expiration of tho legally fixed time after the serving of tile summons. This does nut exclude the possibility of there being defects in the serving of the summons, which, like all other questions concerning tho formalities of the case, must he decided upon by tho Supremo-Court, when the case has been brought before the court. ad 3. No reason has been found for not making the enactments in the 2 of the draft also applicable to summonses to the Supremo-Court issued before the recording of the law, in such a manner, however, that the time, within which the neoessary steps are to be taken, must be reckoned from the time of tbe recording of the law in these islands.

ON MATTERS AND THINGS GENERALLY, BY E. A. HEILBUTH. 3. |Lu » & i. d. AOW. Just as I was waiting to see if nobody else should be sufficiently roused on account of the last election here, to give expression to his sense of the gross abuses connected with that election, I was glad to perceive the communication in this paper of the 18th instant. Yet, the matter is too grave not to require a more searching investigation in all its hearings, than what is contained in this communication, and for that reason 1 will make it the subject matter of this chapter of my disquisitions. It would seem that the persons who took the lead at the elections held here on the 8th instant

of members to the Colonial Council, could hav« had no other aim, than to verify and confirm all that was said in my recent articles on this Council, yea, eveu to lower the Council deeper iu the public estimation, than was my purpose. 1 tried to show it merely as cumbrous and useless, þÿ they have succeeded iu making it contemptible and ridiculous, they have contrived to make it a mere prppet-show, of which a couple of persons hold the wires. This is no metaphor, it is literally true that three or four persons commanding a host of managers, town-agents, cleiks, shop-keepers, tradesmen, ij-e. Sf-o made out a list of the persons they wished to ho elected, and handing it to their dependants, ordered tin m to vote by that ticket. This is our franchise, a great boon, indeed, to voters so situated, a very valuable political right to the Colony, when two or three persons combined can deprive the citizens of it, and use it or abuse it for their own purposes. But the voters, it will ho said, are not hound to follow such a command, they can vote as they please ; ask the wire pullers, and they a will tell you so. But, if true, the answer is ouly Jesuitical truth, which is equal to ten falsehoods, and more false withal than they. The voters are indeed not bound to obey this kind of orders, hut they are not the less compelled to act upon them. If they would all rebel against them, then well and good ; but, woe to the two or three managers who should make the beginning and set the example of voting as they choose, for

Now, should the Colonial Council he kept alive for a while longer, whether in one body, or as two separate Councils, then it will be absolutely necessary to effect such alterations a in true electoral law, as will make the franchise the right, and not, ns now, a humbug and a shameful abuse. To think that the reflections of the will alone be able to counteract the evil, is a vain thought, when we consider the contempt alike of publio opinion and of common decency, with which a few persons, to gratify their own vanity and self interest, forced their I own obnoxious selves into the Council. It will be necessary so to alter the law, as to allow every taxpayer a vote, and that vote, by ballot. For, the objections commonly urged against this system of voting in members, are as nothiug compared to the evil of a Coumil elected in obedience to a few persons holding the voters iu their power, and little-minded enough to use that power, or uuahle to reflect soundly upon the wrong, they commit in observing it. I would also propose the alteration to he effected in the electoral law, that, as is the ease itr Denmark after the example of Great Britain, tbe candidates for membership shall offer themselves as such to the voters. This will obviously serve to restrict the existing abuses, by rendering them very difficult of perpetration, the candidate who proposes himself and his political friends having of course an eye to the machinations of their adversaries, whom, thanks to this

measure, they will know betimes. As things are now, there is no remedy against such abuses, but an alteration in the law of elections, and, of course, the untiring vigilauco of the press. We cannot even cany our complaints of such abuses before the Colonial Conn cil, which according to the Colonial law has the decide thereon, for we would then make to very persons we incriminate, judges upon their own actions and upon our complaints of them, | and we may be sure, that our demand, be it ever so well substantiated, for disqualifying any member of the Council thus elected, w ill be laughed to scorn by the very Council. The Communication above alluded to, is a protest against the result of the last election in Christiansted, protesting against this election being considered as the reflex of the feelings and wishes of the Community, protesting against the new members being hold to be elected by the free and unbiased popular voice, whereas they must be regarded as mere no minces of a few individuals ordering their dependants to the poll. I endorse this protest, and in doing so, I j express the sentiments of a great number of ! voters, by whom I am authorized to do so. To be continued.

The law dated 30th November 1857, in virtue of which Baptism is no longer to he a necessary condition for the right of inheritance, shall be. applicable iu the Danish Westindia Possessions.

The Motives oil which this draft of an Ordinance is based, are, as follows : According to the Danish Code, 5th book 2 chapter 30th and 31st articles, no child could inhci it before it bad been baptized. This enactment taken from the old dnnislt laws might frequently be disadvantageous to i lie parents, pat ticulnrly in case of the mother dying in childbid before the child ; for, if the child had not been baptized, it could not inherit from the mother, and her fortune was then inherited by her other relations ; whereas the child, if it had been baptized, would have inherited Irom the mother, so that her fortune, at the death of the child, would t all to the father. At the same time that the Rescript of t lie 6th April 1831 5 extended the Ordinance of the 30th May 1828 to the Danish Westindia islands, and enacted, that children, whose parents belonged to the evangelical-lutheran church, were in St. Croix and St. Thomas to be baptized within 8 weeks, and in St. Johns within 4 months after their birth, þÿ the 6th section of said Rescript also extended to these islands the Ordinance of tho 4th June 1828. and thereby modified the Danish þÿCode 5-2-30, s 31 in such a manner, that a child, even if it should die without baving been baptized, was not to bo considered excluded from inheritance, if only the time, within which the lawordained that it should be baptized, in suclt cases where a Unfitted lime as the abovo for being baptized was ordained, had not expired before its death.

In accordance with the principles laid down in the Constitutional Law ot Denmark, tho law of the 4th Maoch 1857 has repealed those coercive measures enacted by tho Ordinance of 30th May 1828 to compel parents to have their children baptized within a certain time, enacting at tho same time, however, that parents are, under penalty ot a fine, to report within a certain time the birth of a child to the clergyman of the parish. In consequence of the

change thus introduced, tlie law of 30th November 1857 has ordained as follows : 1. The enactment contained in the Danish þÿCode 5th s book, 2nd chapter, 30th, 31st articles, together with the Ordinal ce of 4th June 1828, viz : that Baptism shall be a necessary condition for the right of inheritance, is hereby repealed Nor shall the omission of reporting, as required by law, the birth of a child to the clergyman of the parish, cause the forfeiture of the right of inheritance. 2. This present law shall exercise no influence on decisions of questions as, to the right of inheritance from persons already deceased, or as to such light of inheritance which depends on the right of inheritance possessed by persons already deceased. Although the law of the 4tli March 1857, as being only one of a series of law's by which in tho mother-country the organisation of the church, as ordained in the Constitutional Law, is being effected, is not adapted to bo extendrd to the Danish Westindia Possessions, and the law of 30tli November 1857 was made necessary by the former, yet it has been deemed most proper to extend this latter law' to these islands, in the same manuer as the Ordinance of 4th June 1828 was extended. The Rescript of the 6th April 1831 4 fixed only with regatd to the evangelical-lutheran congregation a certain time within which children were to be bapj tized, and it is well known, that the lutheran clergymen in these islasds have never been very strict in enforcing baptisms within the

limited time, if the baptism of the child was only not put off for too long a time, and tlieie is hardly sufficient reason to introduce greater severity for the future in this respect. It has been under consideration, if, in extending the law to these islands, a particular i dato should bo fixed for its coming in force in these islands, ns otbctwsse, particularly with regard to the enactment iu 2 concerning the right of inheritance from persons deceased, the question might be raised, as to w hether thereby was to be understood, such ns had died befote the 30th November 1857, but not those that had died in the interval between the latter date and the date of the emanation of the Ordinance for tho Danish Westindia Possessions. The | Government would, however, observe, that two different modes of proceeding may bo adopted in extending, in accordance with the 2ud of the Colonial þÿlaw , laws given for the Mother-country, to tho Danish Westindia Possessions. The Ot (finance for these Islands can either recapitulate the entire contents of the Law, or confine itself to enact, that the Law shall he applicable here. Which of these modes is followed, is, however, in reality immaterial, as the latter mode of proceeding is only adopted for the sake of conciseness. That the contents

of the Law, even when the last-named mode of proceeding is adopted, must be considered as having been, word for word, recapitulated, under date of the Ordinance, by which the contents receive a new application in a territory in which they previously were not applicable, results, not only from the general principle that a new law only acts with regard to to the future, but also from the fact, that this mode of proceeding lias been followed in the Royal Rescripts by which the Ordinances for the Mother-country were extended to the Westindia Possessions in the years from 1821 to 1848. It will also be seen, that the law of 4th January 1854 has extended the Placard of the 10th April 1841, concerning the proper publication of decrees by which persons that are of age are placed under tutelage, to the FierOo Islands, without fixing any particular date, although 3 of the Plaoard treats of persons who, previously to the 10th of April 1841, had been placed under tutelage, while the enactment fui the Fteroo Islands, as a matter of course, is applicable to all persons who, previously to the 4th January 1854, had been placed uuder tutelage. On the other hand it is necessary to adopt a new date in au Ordinance for the Westindia Possessions, when a certain date is named in the Law for tho Mother-country, but which is not adapted to the time of its being extended to these Islands, cfr. the Rescript of 31st December 1818 7.

TUESDAY, 8th NOVEMBER, 1859. þÿ þÿ The Colonial Council will be convened on Saturday the 19th inst St. Thomas will again be unrepresented ; lor, although another election was to þÿ iave been held on Friday last, no one, as we have learnt from a reliable source, appeared at (ho poll. The members for this Island, and those for St. Johns, together with the Crown-Members, a list of whom is published officially in another part of this paper, will comprise the Colonial Council at its fourth Session. Many dralts have been prepared by Government to be discussed by the Council. As far as we are enabled to judge from those already published in this paper, the larger number consists of amendments of laws previously in existence, which have been found necessary to suit the advanced state of civilization in the mothercountry ; and are now proposed to meet a want from a similar cause iu these Colonies. They will, no doubt, occupy the greater part of the time during which the Couucil will be in Session, to the exclusion of private and other hills which members may dectn necessary to bring in At the last Sessiou in 1856, lor instance, tb> bill regulating the position ot the Colonies in the Mother-Country, occupied the greater pan. of the period allotted for the Council to remain in Session, to no purpose at all. Long and dab orate documents wete prepared ; and the Cour. cil had barely time to arrive at a result, when a change in tile Ministeiial organization in Den mark made its labour almost useless. There

were many useful measuies passed, in a hurried manner, at the close of the Session ; but we have never heard of them since. They were smothered, we suppose. The Colonial Council comprises amongits mem bers some men of talent and ability, and who have great interests at stake iu this Island particularly. There are also some facile members þÿ a very necessary ingredient, since they enable the leading members to oblatD majorities, when the voting takes place. Iu fact, the Council is at present well-constituted; and we titist our hopes of it will not be disappointed. Only let the working members endeavour to pass one or (wo useful measures þÿ measures that the community desire þÿ and this community will look upon them in the light of public benefactors. Let them endeavour to obtain for us religious freedom ; so that when our daughters, or others, feel inclined to worship God in a manner different

from that which they before employed, they shall not be subject to legal investigations (or perhaps we should rather say inquisitions) and annoyance. Let them obtain for us the freedom of the press; so that our community may become enlightened; and let them not continue to confound cause and effect, and suppose that we should become enlightened first, before we make use of this powerful means of enlightenment. Dare we hope that this session will not be altogether barren of good 5

The activity consequent on the arrival and departure of the several Mail Backets within the last few days, has removed from the mind of every business man all thought of local politics. But as there is a lull to-day, it would be well to know whether something could not be done to set aside, once for all, this vexed question of a Colonial Council, which to us in its present form, has a strong similarity to the man who is inconsiderately pressed to come to his neighþÿbours feast, when it is neither agreeable nor convenient to accept. As it is then clear, in the language of the play, that þÿ something must be þÿdone, it were time we made a beginning. Now it has been pretty generally proposed that for the election of Friday next a ticket be handed round to the voters with Mr. JIeilbutii at the head, a.,d the names of such other gentlemen as it is supposed could be absent for a few days, and that or, the assembling of the Council, they would there make known the unanimous wish of St. Thomas ; first, to have a separate Council, and that a legislative one. This measure could he materially strengthened by a petition to the King, to be laid before the Council ; and this would be easy to accomplish, seeing that such a document has been prepared since 1851, and is now lying at the office of one of our Merchants, to which there could ba added, in addition to those already subscribed, an extension of signatures. To this appeal we should say that llis Majesty would most certainly concede, as it is pro-
posed in the very first paragraph of the law. Let þÿ something be þÿdone so that we escape from our present anomalous position.

(Continued ) The Motives on which the preceding draft is based are as follows : On a bill for regulating the Country Schools in St. Croix being introduced, by a private member, in the third session of the Colonial Council, the Council addressed a request to tho Government, soliciting that the necessary steps might be taken for laying before the Council, in its next session, a draft of an Ordinance regulating the schools in St. Croix, based upon the principles laid down in tho abovementioned private bill, viz : 1.) Abolition of the Saturday Schools, 2.) The division of tho children into 2 classes to be instructed on different days of the week, combined with an extended term of years for attending school, and as far as feasible, also with more ample instruction. The Government having obtained the opinions of the Inspector of Schools and of tne Chairman in the Sohoolcommissiou concerning the matter, and a Draft of an Ordinance, modifying and adding several clauses to the Or-

St. 8 i Q> S X A V l) 3. dinance of the 6th September 1853 for the regulation of the Country Schools in the Danish Westindia Possessions having been laid belore the abovementioned School-commission, þÿ the preceding Draft was drawn up which, in all essential points, is in accordance with the opinions obtained. The abovementioned request from the Colonial Council, regarding the abolition of Saturday Schools, had, as will be seen from the draft by which the request was occasioned, as well as from the report of the committee of the Colonial Council, reference to the Saturday Schools for the older children of the age of 10 to 13 years, prescribed by 3 and 4 of the Ordinance of 6ih September 1853, and in which instruction is given during 4 hours of the forenoon, on the one mentioned day of the week, the children not attending school on the other days of the week. It must be considered as proved by experience that these Saturday Schools, at all events in most places, have not answered to this purpose, viz : not only to keep up the information imparted to the children from their 6th to their 10th year in the five-days schools, but also of further developing the same ; to which may further be added the circumstance noticed in the report of the abovementioned Committee, that it is of special interest to the parents to have their older children exempted from attending school on Saturdays, as higher wages are given on these days than on any other of the week, which causes the Saturday Schools to be more neglected

than the Schools kept on the other live days of the week. From these reasons the abolition of the now existing Saturday Schools has been recommended in all the opinions, obtained by Government on the subject ; and these have on the other hand advised tho introduction of schools to be held three separate days of the week, as well for the older as for the youDger children with 6 hours daily instruction, Saturday to he one of the days on which the younger children shall attend school, instead of school to be held three þÿday o s f the week for the younger children of the ago of from 6 to 9 years, and schools to be, held two days of the week for the older children of the age of from 9 to 12 years, as advised in the private bill introduced in the Colonial Council. The Government is also of the opinion, that this is the only way in which more ample instruction in the Country Schools is to be obtained, which the Colonial Council has considered requisite, in order that the instruction should reach that standard which ought under all circumstances to be attained. As it will generally only be childicn from 6 to 9 years of age, who are to attend school on Saturdays, neither the interests of the parents nor of the planters, will thereby be interfered with ; and as the children will not leave school before 3 þÿo clock p. in., instead of 12 þÿo clock, as hitherto, the want of control over them during the greatest part of the day, in the absence of the parents, at work in the field, or in the market, þÿ which want has also

been advanced as an argument against the now existing þÿSaturday Schools þÿ will also, in a great measure, be met by the alteration proposed. According to the plan of instruction established by the Ordinance of the 6th September 1853, the children are to attend the Country Schools in St. Croix from their 6th to their 10th year, 5 days weekly, each day 4 hours, which, deducting Sundays and vacations, gives 940 hours yearly, and for 4 years 3760 hours. They are then transferred to the Saturday Schools until they attain their 13th year; in these instructions is given on 47 Saturdays of the year 4 hours on each of these days, which gives 188 hours yearly, and in 3 years 564 hours. The total amount of hours for instruction in the Country Schools at present is consequently 4,324 hours. If the Saturday Schools were altogether abolished, according to the private bill laid be- ' fore the Colonial Council, &Dd attendance at schools three days of the week introduced for children up to their 9th year and two days of the week for children up to their 12th year, every child would receive instruction in 4,230 hours; but as, according to the opinion of tho Inspector of 8choo)s, experience has fully hewn, that instruction every second day is not as productive, as instruction roceived for several days in succession, it i» to be feared, that the result would be that the children

would make less progress in the schools than hitherto. According to the preceding Diaft the children will on the contrary receive insti union lor 6 years, on 3 days of the week, 6 hours every day, which gives a total of 5076 horns of instruction, consequently 758 hours more than according to the now existing plan of instruction It is to be expected, that this increase in the term of instruction will not only make up for the abovementioned diff r. nee between instruction every day and instruction every second day, but will even, togeth r with the new enactments contained in the Draft, for the prevention of non-attendanee at school, &c., materially conti ibute to make the whole instruction more effective In accordance with the opinion expressed in the ahovemeutioned Report of the Committee of the Colonial Council in the 3id Session, that it would he necessary to oblige the children to attend the Sunday schools of the respective congregations to which they belong until they attain their 15ih year of age, and as the Schoolcommissions have also advised this, an enactment to this effect has been introduced in the Dralt. The following remarks are offered to the special of the Draft. ad 1. According to the Ordinance of the 6th September 1853 2 þÿnew pupils are admitted to the schools once a year, viz ; in the beginning of the month of October, and, according to 1, no child must be admitted before having attained its 6th year. In eonsequeuce hereof some children ate without schooling until they have

nearly filled their 7th year. In the same manner, the enactment contained in 19. that tho final dismissal from school shall likewise only take place once a year, has obliged some children to continue their attendance at school until they have almost filled their 14th year, although 3 enacts, that the attendance shall cease when the children have attained their 13th year. In Older to remedy this, and as it can not be considered advisable to admit children to the school belore they have attained their 6th year, even if only a few months should be wanting to complete this age, it is enacted in the Draft, that admittance, as well as dismissal shall in future take place twice every year. It has furthermore been found advisable to enact that the public examinations in the schools, with which the dismissal from school and the admittance of new pupils is closely connected, should take place in the month of June, instead of, as hitherto, the month of September, whereby the delay with regard to admittance of children in the schools immediately after the public examinations will be avoided, which delay is at present necessitated by the removals that take place among tho laborers iu the month of October. ad 2. The enactment contained in t lie Ordinance of the 6th Septe mber 1853 I. according to which children on estates are exempted from attending the Country Schools, when they receive satisfactory instruction by any other means, is, however, liable to abuse ou account of the present want of control with such in-

struction, the children perhaps being employed all day in domestic services, or in the pasture, under the pretext of being instructed out of the Country Schools, or the parents, or the private teachers concerned, allowing the children to neglect the school to such a degr. c, as to learn almost nothing. It has therefore been found necessary to enact that the Sehoolcom mission shall decide, whether the repot ted in struction can in reality be considered sufficient, and that the Inspector of Schools, whoso posi tion affords him the best opportunity of becoming acquainted with the circumstances in such cases, shall be afforded opportunity to give his opinion concerning such cases ; and also, that, according to circumstances, it may be stipulated as a condition, that such children must be sent to be examined in the Country Schools. If such a child attends a licensed private school where public examination is held or if the Schoolcommi-sion otherwi.-e feels convinced of the progress of the child, it shall, however, as a matter of course, not bo necessary that it should be examined in the Country Schools.
