LUMBAR I) Y. FROM the þÿtimes correspondent. MILAN, Oct. 8. The m"'f I see of Milan and the Milanese the " tiiti'f my first impression is strengthened. M ;u he turbulent is happy and confiding, as it, perhaps, never has been before, and this state ot joyful satisfaction is fully reflected by the outdoor life and movement, of the town. Although the greater part of the rich people are i at their country seats one scarcely remarks their absence, so animated is that which remains. Besides this the town has become a rendezvous for strangers and a place of pilgrimage for Italians from all parts of the Peninsula, especially Piedmont and Centra! Italy The influx would be even gieatcr were it not for the want of accommodation at the hotels, which þÿdon suffice t to harbour them. Most of the fir-t-rate hotels are obliged to send away not a few who have not taken the precaution to bespeak rooms by the telegraph. Above all, for the last few days the throng was great, for the day after to-morrow the races are to take place, at which the King is to be present. You may remember they were forbidden under the Austrian rule, and have not taken plane for some years The consequence is that they excite much more interest than they very likely would have done otherwise. Yet, in spite of all this movement and life in the town, you never saw a more orderly and well-behaved population. Let any one who labours under the delusion that it is ouly Englishmen who can govern themselves, and be kept

quiet without gendarmes, come to this place and he will be astouished and convinced of bis error. | The town, which under the Austrian rule could only be kept moderately quiet by armed sentries walking up and down the main thoroughfares, now takes care of itself. For hours you can walk about without seeing any of the cockedhat representatives of authority ; and for hours likewise you may walk about and see not the slighest disturbance in all this crowd. Audyet there are many points in which it is densely packed, as before the cafes listening to i'inerant minstrels, or gazing at Punchinello's exhibitions, or the display of quacks and þÿcharlatans. Towards the eveuiug alone the patrols of the National Guard begin to pice the streets, but they seem there more for their own amusement than for any use þÿ at least, f have never seen their services in the least required. This institution of the National Guard has progressed more in Milan than in any other town ot Lombardy. I am told that there are not. less than 12,000 enrolled and doing service. That the institution is highly popular you can see by looking at the first guardhouse you pass, or at the first detachment of them which passes you Numbers of men between 40 and 50, with an unmistakable ,l air þÿbourgeois about them, show that the rage has attacked the most sober part of the population. #»«

The most astonishing fact, however, in this state of things is the almost total absence of any feelings of vindictiveness against those who formerly were supporters and agents of the Austrian Government. It is as if the past sufferings had all been forgotten in the present joy and happiness. Numbers of Germans who have been established here still remain, and are unmolested, except, perhaps, now and then by a harmless joke; nay, even those wcliknown agents of the secret police

eiim a « n su of Austria who had the death of more than one individual and the misery of more than oue fa- | luily on their conscience have, with one or that two exceptions, escaped unharmed. The fact is what their very impoh nee protects them, and was formerly an object of terror has become an object of ridieulo now. Tiius, oue who was well known for his Austrian tendencies, and thought it prudent to couceal himself on his property on the Lake of Como, had a practical joke played him which frightened him out of the country. He was known to be in communication with a priest living iu the neighbourhood, aud this priest ; was told that the place of concealment of the | fugitive was known, and that the latter would be attested shortly. The priest, of course, did not fail to acquaint the concealed man with the danger that threatheued him, and the result was that the latter was the same day over the Swiss frontier, where a day or two alter he received oue of the local humouiistic papers, sout to his address, aud containing a detailed account of the joke which had hem played off on him. Ho has returned since to Milan, where he remains , without any notice being taken ol him. And yet the Austrians had done enough during the last 10 years to drive the people almost to madness i and excite that feeling of vindictiveness for which all Italians get such ample credit. Knowing their unpotrifle a popular demonstration, which pularity and constantly suspecting, they was saw in every to be put down by arrests and condemnations. And yet so

their engines of terror powerless were they iu that all their might and with all they could not prevent a regular understanding between Piedmont aud Lombardy which existed long before the war was declared. The system of terror produced the very þÿefl ectwhich it was to have prevented and contributed more than anything else to unite all Lombards. A hat worn colour side of the head or the other, a glove of one on one or another, a |<eculiar colour, a riband þÿ in fact, any trifle, was made into a sign of the union in feeling, I ikke and made the duties of the Austrian police hard and ineffective. But the thing which showed more than anything else this union was that of a premature break could be prevented in spite the excitement outwhich prevailed when the political affairs began to be complicated. Several times the leaders had to use all their influence to prevent this danger, which might have compromised the whole cause. And fortunate it was, for a good deal of this orderly and sober bohavi- : our of the population is probably due to the circumstance that the transition from one regime to the other tool; place without any participation of the people, llad this not been the case, it would have been impossible to keep down altogether the bad passions which a popular outbreak carries invariably in its wake. As it was, Milan awoke one morning and found itself free. The unanimity of hatred against the Austrians has now changed into a similar unanimity of love to Piedmont, to whom tho Lombards look up as

their deliverer. It is most wonderful to witness the attachment and confidence winch reigns here towards that country and the King. Scarcely among the disappointed suitors for places do be you any other feeling. It would untrue to say that no find the traces of one sees the tardiness winch the Government displays ; but such is the confidence that very lew think it worth

seem that the Government knows host what it does, and all will be right in the end. This blind confidence is so much tile more remarkable, as there is a general impression that before long the war with Austria will be renewed. Beautilul as it is to witness such unbounded confidence, one cannot help feeling that it i" in some measure due to the system of oppression and blind obedience to which the country lias been accus. tonied by the Austrians and a consequent want of political education and interest. The Lombards have been so accustomed to see all the acts of the Government shrouded by a veil of secrosy that they think tins qmlity inseparable from any Government j they have been so long deprived of any participation in tho Government t lint they Imvc not become yet aware of the fact that they may Imve some business themselves with it. They arc young yet, and so happy to have got rid of the Austrians that they leave all the rest to tho Government. There will come, no doubt, a time when they will feel that however popular and lull of goodwill a Government may be, it is prone to go to sleep and to take false steps unless it is kept up to the mark. Were it not for this an absolute popular Government would be no doubt the most perfect. But, alas ! since the fabulous golden age when Saturn ruled these kind of paternal Governments have considerably degen. Prated. While this illusion lasts let Lombardy be happy, no one will grudge her her good time after so much hard suffering.

The case calls for the attention of proprietors and aitorncys ; in order that the condition of this class of deserving persons may be ameliorated. We believe the remedy to be applied consists in the separation of the yearly payment for feeding the it Overseer from the þÿManager S s alary, leaving optional to the Overseer to take his meals at the þÿManager table, s or to furnish himself. The grasping avarice displayed by many Managers, in their desire to accumulate wealth rapidly, is, in almost every case, gratified at the expense of the poor overseer. We have beard of cases, whore, although the overseer was fed at the þÿManager table, s a different meal was served up j for the former than that served up, after he had left, for the latter. This very mean and unjust proceeding ought to bo prevented ; and this cau only be done by the interference of proprietors or attorneys.

JOHAN FRED ERIK SCHLEGEL, Gouverneur over de dansk vestindiake Besiddelser, Ridder af Dannebrog, Gjor vitterligt: Paa Grund af de stedfindende Forhold finder jeg mig foranlediget til, i Kraft afden mig ved Coloniallovens 4 givne Myndighed, ved denne forelobige Anordning at fastsiette oganordne som folger: I Latidskolerne paa St. Croix optages Underviisning i Skrivning og Syning blandt de almindelige Lieregjenstande, saaledes, at samme for Fremtiden meddeles udeii soerligt Vederlag paa de Tider, der af Skolecommissionen bestemmes for disse Underviisningsfag.

MOTIVERNLi til foranstaaemle forelobige Anordning ere saalydenile : Efterat det i 15 af Anordningen af Gte September 1853 angaaende Reglement for Latidskolerne paa de dansk vestindiske tier var blevet fastsat, at Underviisning i Skrivning og Syning blev at meddele de Born, hvis Foraeldre ville betale derfor, blev der fra Skolebestyrelsernes Side paa St. Croix foretaget det Muligste for at gjflre Underviisningen i disse Lairegjenstande alniindelig og frugtbringende snart viste skoler. Ligesom det imidlertid i Oens Landsig, at de Bidrag, der ydedes af ended af Skolebornenes Forseldre, ingeiilunde vare tilstraekkelige til derined at bestride Liinningen til en Liererinde i Syning ved liver | Skole, og til Anskaflelse af de liodvendige Materialier til Underviisning i begge Laeregjenstande, saaledes gjordes der efterhaanden den Erfaring, at Underviisningen i samme i de tleste Skoler var lidet Irugtbringende, paa Grund af, at Foricldrenes Bidrag erlagdes hoist uregelmiessigt, livorved foranledigedes idelige Afbrydelser i de vedkommende Borns Underviisning i de omhandlede Fag. Af disse Grunde foresloge Landskolecommissionerne paa for Croix allerede i 1850, at Betalingen St. Underviisning i Skrivning og Syning niuntte bortlalde, og at en Liererinde inaatte ant ages og lonnes at Landkassen ved liver af Skolerne, med Forpligtelse til at here Pigebbrnene Syning saint til at assistere Licrerne ved den Ovrige Underviisning. Da Bestemnielsen om sierlig Betaling for Underviisning i Skrivning og Syning

var grundet saavel i den Betragtning, at disse Lieregjenstande ikke egentlig kutide ansees at ligge indenfor Forniaalet af den almindelige Underviisning i de offentlige Landskoler her paa Oerne, som paa det Onskelige i, at Landarbeiderne, der oeko- befinde sig under saa sterdeles gode her nomiske Vilkaar, bleve bragte til at indsee, at de ikke have Krav paa, at dot Offentlige skal gjiire Alt for dein uden at fordre uogen Anstriengelse eller Vederlag fra deres Side, þÿ maatte det vistnok ansees tvivlsomt, hvorvidt der var tilstiaekkelig Anledning til at foretago en Forandriug i Anordningens Forskrift i den omhandlede Henseende. St. Croix Borgerraad udtalte imidlertid den Anskuelse, at det, foruden hvad der i Aliiiindelighed taler for Udbrcdelseti af nyttige Kundskaber, i Sserdeleshed her var vigtigt snarest muligt at gjftre saadanne Kundskaber saa almindelige, at Besiddelsen af samine ikke Isenger skulde kunne ansees at gjbrc Vedkommende for gode til at soge deres Erhverv ved Agerdyrkningeti,

derstedse maa blive Hovedbeskjafftigelsen for den Deel af Befolkningen, hvorom her er Sporgsinaal. Da derhos Skrivning og Syning vare optagne blandt de almindelige Underviisningsgjenstande i de offentlige Skoler i Byerue og den hidtilvierende Forskjel i denne Henseende med Ilensyn til Landskolerne afgav et Paaskud for Landbefolkningen til at sende deres Born til Byerne, indstillede Borgerraadet, at Landskolecommissionernes Forslag maatte blive taget tilfblge, og at den fornodne Forandring i Anordningen af Ote September 1853 15 maatte skee ved en af Gouvernementet udgiven foreliibig Anordning. Gouvernenientet inaatte ogsaa vaere al den Anskuelse, at der var overvei ude Gruude tilstede til at optage Skrivning og Syning blandt de almindelige Lseregjenstande i Landskolerne. Naar Anordningen af Gte September 1853 har gjort Underviisningen i disse Fag afhiengig af sserlig Betaling fra Bbruenes Forieldre, er det dog derved bleven forudsat, at det ogsaa under denne Betingelse vilde blive muligt, at give ialtfald den allerstorste Deel af Bornene Underviisning deri ; men dette havde Erfaringen viist ikke at kunne opnaaes. Det Offentlige inaatte under al le Omstaendigheder yde et ikke ubetydcligt Bidrag til Underviisningen i disse Fag lor det irnlskrienkede Antal Born, hvis Forieldre ydede Betaling, om endog uregelmiessigt, og llesultatet af den for de enkelte Born idelig afbrudte Underviisuing blev alligevel hoist ringc. Ved med en forholdsviis mind re betydelig ForOgelse af det þÿOfl entliges Ud-

gift at gjore Skrivning til en almindelig Lieregjenstand i Landskolerne, vilde der derimod opnaaes, at saiume vilde blive et vaesentligt Hjaelpemiddel til alle Bornenes grumligere Underviisning i Laesning, idet deres egen Iver for og Evne til Fremgang i Lsesning i hoi Grad foroges, naar de kunne begynde at skrive. Hvad Syning angaaer er en vis Faerdiglied i samme sau fornodent for ethvert Fruentimmer, ogsaa af Landalmuen, at det maatte ansees Ira enliver .Side ligtigt, at aabtie Adgang lor alle Pigebornene til Underviisning deri. Af disse Grunde og tillige i Betragtning at de af Borgerraadet udluevede OmstaMidigheder, og da det maatte ansees sierdeles Onskeligt, at Forandringen kunde indfbres ved det nye Skoleaars Begyndelsc i Efteraaret 1857, blev den foranstaaende forelobige Anordning af Iste November 1857 udgivet: og þÿ det foreslaaes herved : at Underviisning i Skrivning og .Syning fremdeles gives i Laudskolcnie paa St. Croix uden sierlig Betaling af Bornenes Foraeldre, i Overeensstemmelse med $ G af det Colonial ruadet forelagte Udkast til en Anordning mdeholdende Forandring og luermere Bestemmelser af Anordningen af Gt.e September 1853 angaaende Reglement for Landskolerne paa <le dansk vestindiske Oer.

JOIIAN FREDERIK SCIILEGEL, Governor of the Danish Westindia Posses sions, Knight of Dannebrog, Maketh known : That in consideration of the present circumstances, I have found it ex

pedieut, iti virtue of ths power invested in me by the fourth of the Colonial Law, by this provisional Ordinance to enact and ordain : In the Country-Schools in St. Croix writing and needle-work shall be included among the ordinary branches of instruction, and shall in future be taught without payment, at such times the Schoolcoinmission may decide. The Motives on which the preceding provisional Ordinance is based are as follows : After it had been enacted in 15 of the Ordinance of the 6th September 1S53 for the regulation of Country-Schools in the Danish Westindia Possessions, that instruction in writing and needle-work should be given to children, whose parents were willing to pay for it, every thing possible was done by the directors of the schools in St. Croix, in order that the instruction in these branches might become general and productive in the Country-Schools. But in the same manner as it soon became evident that the contiibutiuns made by some of the þÿchildren s parents were in no wise sufficient to afford a salary to a female teacher in needlework in each school, and to cover the expenses for the materials requisite for instruction in both branches, experience likewi.-e soon proved that the instruction in this respect was of little use, as, on account of the irregulaiity of the payment on the part of the parents, the instruction of the children iu these branches was frequently interrupted. From these reasons the Schoolcomtnisaions iu St. Croix proposed alrea-

dy in the year 1850 that the payment for instruction iu writing anil needle-work should be done away with, and that a female teacher should bo appointed in each of the schools, and remunerated from the Landtreasnry, who should instruct the gills in needle-work and assist the teaehers in the other brauches of instruction. As the enactment relative to payment for instruction iu writing and ucedle-work was based, as well on the consideration, that these brandies could not properly bo included iu the design for tho general instruction iu the public Country-Schools in those islands, as in tho desire that tho rural population?, who are under so very favorable pecuniary circumstances, should be made to understand, that they have no right to claim that the public should do every thing for them, without any exertion or remuneration being required of them, þÿ it might certainly be considered doubtful, whether there was sufficient reason to make an alteration in the enactment of the Ordinance in this respect. The Burgher Council iu St. Croix was , however, of the opinion, that besides the general reasons that speak in favor of a diffusion of useful knowledge, it was cspocially of importance here, that sucli knowledge should, as soon as po.-sibl , become so general, that the parties in possession of it could no longer consider themselves to be too goud to earn their livelihood by agriculture, which ought constantly to be the chief employment of that part of the population in question here. And a . writing and

needle-work had been included among the usual branches of instruction in tho public Schools in the towns, and the hitherto existing difference in this respect in tho Country Schools afforded a pretext for the rural population to send their children to the towns, the Burgher Council requested, that the proposal made by the Country-Schoolcoiumissions should he adopted, and that the necessary alteration in the Ordinance of the 6th September 1853 15 should bo effected by a provisional Ordinance from Government. The Government had alro come to the conclusion, that there were weighty reasons in favor of admitting writing and needle-work among tho general branches of instruction iu tho Country Schools. When it was enacted in the Ordinance of the 6th September 1853, that instruction in these branches should be dependant on payments from the parenls of the children it was also presumed, that it would have been possible, even on this condition, to give at least the majority of the children instruction in them ; but experience has shewn that this was not attainable. The Public had under all circumstances to make considerable contributions towards the instruction in these branches for that limited number of children, whose parents paid for the instruction, if even irregularly, and the result of the instruction, iu

$ in. e $ a (i x «s yy » » which each child was continually interrupted, was, nevertheless, very insignificant. By making, at a trifling increase in t lie expenses of ihe Public, writing one of the ordinary branches of instruction in tin- Country-Schools, this would, on the contrary, become an essential help in imparting a more thorough inst> uction in reading, the zeal and ability of the children to improve in tending being in a great degree inct eased when they are able to begin to wiite. A certain degree of expertness in needle-wo k is so necessary for every female, even atnoDg tire rural population, that it must be con-idered in every respect, proper, that opportunity should be given to all t he girls ot being instructed in this branch. From these reasons and in consideration of the circumstances mentioned by the Burgher Couucil, and as it was considered very desirable that the alteration could be introduced at t lie commencement of the new School-year in the autumn ot the year 1857, the preceding provisional Otdinance of 1st Novi tuber 1857 was published ; and it is hereby proposed : that instruction in writing and needle-work shall continue to be given in the Country- Schools in St. Croix without any special payment from the par-nts of the children, in accordance with 6 of the Draft of an Ordinance laid before t he Colonial Council, modifying and making several additions to the Oidinanee of the 6th September 1853, for regulating the Country-Schools in the Danish w estiudia Possessions.

FRIDAY, 18th NOVEMBER, 1859. - ' in proportion asserted 1 1 lias been as the structure ol a government by a great statesman, that gives loroo to public opinion, it is essential that public opinion should be þÿenlightened. In granting to the culonies a representative institution, however imperfect that institution may be, it was, undoubtedly, the intention of the homegovernment, that public opinion should have some weight in our future government. The existence of such an opinion has but recently begun to manifest itself; and, but for the want of enlightenment, its progress would have been more rapid. But no enlightenment can be obtained as long as a system of secrecy and public exelusion in regard to public affairs is maintained. Ml our institutions are carried on in this manner Our Colonial Council, Burgher Council, public courts, government acts, are all shrouded in secrecy and mystery. Where is the means of obtaining enlightenment on public affairs under such a system ? þÿ Iu the worst-governed þÿcountries says a distinguished writer, þÿ everything is concealed, and a state of infantine and ridiculous imbecility of the national mind is the

» ?. ® ! ® u « v r; , consequence. In the best-governed countries there is no concealment at all ; and the result may be seen in the shrewd wit and large understanding of the þÿAmericans. It is time that this state of things should cease. Investigation on public affairs is a pursuit in which there is everything to hope and nothing to fear. There should be no closed documents iu the public transactions of a community ; no private processes going on, into which tnose whose dearest interests are at stake have no right to intrude. No facts ol publio importance can be profaned by public scrutiny; no evil oan arise from our understanding our own business too well. To this secret system we ascribe all the evils of our government To state one ease clearly. The secret correspondence carried on between the local Government and the home Ministry, and which never transpires, but iu a meagre sketch in the Danish Papers under the head of intelligence from the West India islands, relating principally to the state of the weather and the prevalence or non -prevalence of yellowfever, is the most potent agency, we believe, iu quashing all the useful measures which have from time to time been proposed by the Colonial Council. Yet of this correspondence we never lear.i a word. Now here is a great evil in our system of government þÿ that the wish of an entire public can be frustrated without our over learning by what means or arguments that result may have been obtaiued. Our officials are not fairly entitled to presume that they are wiser than all

the rest of their fellow citizens together; aud whilo they may conscientiously think a measure imprudent, it is hut, just that we should know the reasons why they think so. Our space aud time will not allow us to go further into the question ; but we earnestly hope, that steps will be taken to opeu all our Councils and Commissions to the public ; for, until that is done, we will never advance one step iu the path of a just and wise administration. Some alterations are about to be made iu the Country-School Ordinance. It would bo wise if some member of the Colonial Couucil would propose that the meetings of the School-Commission should be publicly held. When this is done, a great advance townids the improvement of our system of public education iu towu and country, of which it is sadly iu need, will be made.

LIGHT BREAKING ON THE CHINESE QUESTION. Beyond all question the most important doeu. meat which has been publish' d in reference to the recent affair of the Pci-hj iu China, is the letter from our representative, Mr. Ward, published in the New York Times of 1 1 th instant. That letter, it seems, was written on 30th June þÿ five days after the battle þÿ was addressed to a private friend in this couutry, and avas by that friend sent to the Times for publication. We may say, in brief, that it confirms in the fullest manner the view which we have taken of Commodore þÿTattnall s conduct, and places his censors in an unenviable position. Our Chinese correspondent has stated, aud we have indorsed the assertion, that our attitude of neutrality between the maritime powers of Europe and the Chinese lias conferred upon us uo advantage, and has not been recognized by the Chinese ; that we have been indebted to the protection of British guns for the safety of our trade in China, and for the slender opportunity we have enjoyed of concluding a satisfactory treaty. For the evidence in support of the latter proposition we refer to our letter from the Pei-ho, published two weeks ago. The writer of that letter þÿ an officer of high standing in the United States navy þÿ states positively that our representative in China was only able to conclude a treaty last year because the Chinese dared not refuse the demands of one who had such powerful friends as the French and English ; that he ascended the Pei-ho in the wako

of the European fleets, and did his business under shelter of their guns ; that when they left ho was compelled to leave also. The fact can not be dwelt upon with too much stress, as illustrating the value of the neutrality by which our home politicians and editors set such store. Mr. Ward now furnishes additional evidence. Some of the newspapers here have blamed him (aud a newspaper correspondent says that the State Department concurs in the censure) for having mixed himself up with the Europeans in the negotiation. Why did lie not, says an authority which claims to be iuspired in high quarters, proceed to have his treaty ratified without reference to the French and English J Mr. Ward supplies the answer. He says : We were in company with the other Powers, not by our own choice. I had desired to avoid all complication with them ; and to secure this end I had left Hong Kong so immediately after my arrival as to draw ou myself the censure of one of the Hong Kong journals. The Chinese had themselves forced us into our present position, their Commissioners at Shanghai having insisted upon my waiting for the English and French Ministers, and coming with them. In consequence of this we had been incessantly receiving from them acts of courtesy and kindness. Now, should they be successful, we should profit by their success. In opening the road to Pekin to their owu Ministers, they would also opeu it to þÿus. In plain language, the Chinese at the Pei-ho made uo distinction between the Americans aud

the Europeans. They were ready to ratify our treaty, if they ratified the treaties with Great Britain and þÿFrance which they were resolved to evade as long as possible ; but there is not a title of evidence to show that any favors or consideration were reserved for us which were denied to the European allies. Mr. þÿWard s attempt to negotiate separately was at once frustrated by the Chinese. He must, they told him in substance, take his chance with the other outside barbarians. Wc pity Mr. Buchanan if he has allowed the superficial reasoning which lately found vent in our newspapers to induce him to censure Mr. Ward for acting in concert with the representa lives ol England and France. The point of the question, as we stated two weeks since, turns on the truth or falsity of the representation made to Mr. Ward by the Pei-ho officials, to the effect that he aud the other embassadors must proceed to the north mouth of the Pei-ho, where they would find an escoit of rank waiting for them, and prepared to conduct them to Pekin. A correspondent of the Evening Post, writing from Shanghai, stated positively that after the battle Mr. Ward had sent, messengers to this northern mouth, and had iu (.fleet discovered that the Chinese representations were correct, and that ho and his colleagues were anxiously expected there. It was even stated that Mr. Ward had gone to þÿl ekiu That gentleman himself seems singularly unaware of these various proceedings. He says : As 1 would do every thing in my power for

the fulfilment of my mission, I determined to make the effort to reopen negotiations with the OhineseJ, and as soon as possible I sent a letter to the Governor-General of this province, who was said to be somewhere on the coast about ten miles from the forts. Yesterday I dispatched my brother, with the interpreters in search of the place and the man. They left this anchorage in the Toey-wan about 11 a.m., carrying my letter, in which I informed the Governor-General that I was here under the treaty, and by the invitation of the Commissioners at Shanghai ; that I was charged with an autograph letter from the President of the United States to His Majesty the Emperor, and askod him to provide me with means of conveyance to Pekin. The Toey-wan returned at 8 p.m , and my brother tells mo that after going northwest along tho

coast, about ten miles from tbis anchorage, they di'Covered an inlet near a village which was strongly fortified. The 'I'oe.y-wan could not ap- of proach nearer than four miles in consequence the shallowness of the water

midshipman, went ashore in th boat >f the Toeywan. At the approach of the boat the villagers began to fly. They succeeded, however, in bolding communication with two of the Chiuese, who stated that the Governor-General had gone over to the torts at the mouth of the Pci-ho, and said they would deliver the fitter to him. These men said they had never heard of the United States of America, and warned the party that they had better return to their boat, as a large body of cavalry had been sent for, who were Tartar soldiers, and recognized no distinctions among foreign barbarians While they were conversing with the Chinese a large b( dy of cavalry, well mounted, actually appeared in sight, rapidly advancing toward them, and, as they returned to their boat, followed them to the water's edge.'' These Tartar horsemen who þÿ recognize no distinctions among foreign þÿbarbarians aro a delicious commentary upon the advantages of the þÿ neutrality, so highly prized by some of our prints. If Mr. þÿWard sbrother and his friends had not made the best of their way to their boat, it seems that their neutrality would hardly have saved their skins, any more than the United States flag saved American ships in 1857. Had these gentlemen becD massacred þÿ as it seems they would have been had they staid to discuss the question þÿ it would have been curious to see what tins eulogists of our Chinese policy would have said. When Canton was attacked two years ago, the late Governor Yeh declared that for the life of him he could

not distinguish an American from au Englishman, and, therefore, that our fellow-citizens must look out for themselves ; the officials in the north ato, it seems, equally careless of distinctions among the barbarians. Wo repeat what wo said in our last number þÿ the Chinese do not discriminate between the Europeans and ourselves. The Government does not discriminate ; the mandarins do not discriminate; the. people do not discriminate. The advantage which some Government prints pretend that we have gained over the English by our policy of conciliation is imaginary and delusive. We have gained nothing at all, except a saving of money. Aud, while wo aro not prepared to advocate a war with China without more substantial ground for hostilities than at present exist, the fact that the Chinese have always treated us as badly as the most active of their enemies, and that our successes, commercial and diplomatic, in that quarter of the globe, have hitherto been mainly due to the awe struck into the Chiuese mind by the warlike manoeuvres of the Europeans, ought to render people extremely tender of censuring Comraodoro Tattnall for any aid which he may have rendered to thoso who have so often projected us against thoso who have invariably inured us to the full exteut of their capacity.

What people desired, was to be let alone by the Government, and to bo bothered as little as possible, being quite satisfied to be ruled as of old by the king and the laws of Denmark. By an Ordinance of March 31st 1755, the Danish Code and the Danish Laws had been extended to these Colonies, and as they were just aud equitable, they had created satisfaction and confidence in the population. Besides these laws, there was a multitude of local rules aud regulations enacted by almost every Governor, some of them really useful, but for the most part emanations of gubernatorial vanity or folly. Everybody has seen or, at least, heard of the volumes of enactments for the Colonies, issued by the Governors General, the lecture of which in these our days serves to amuse us, at the stupidity of some of them, and to inform us of the forgotten names and deeds of these great legislators. It is a common say, that too many laws are worse than no laws at all. Certain is it, that in these Colonies, what with the Danish laws aud the Colonial ordinances, there was too much law, and the consequence was the usual one. Laws

and ordinances had no sooner been emanated, than they became almost as dead letters. As for the ordinances issued by the Governors, some of them were already null and void at their issuing, and oould not even be enforced by the lej'is'ator himself, nor acknowledged as binding by the Courts. For in order to render such ordinances valid, they required the assent of the king within one year of their omanation, and they next required to be published and recorded by the lawcourts, this publication being, according to ancient laws reinforced by the lloyal Ordinance of October 8th 1824, an indispensable condition for the validity of every law or ordinance. The condition of these Colonies presented nothing analogous to the conditions of any oth r Colonies cither in ancient or modern times, and therefore such institutions as had been adapted to other Colonies and served for their wants and interests, could not be applied to these Islands. It required a profound study of these Islands in all their peculiarities, a study only to he made on the spot, investigating how and by what people these Coloniis were first settled, who are their present inhabitants, and to which different nationalities and religious creeds they belong, in what country they have their natural connexions, and in what manner, or by what ties the separate Islands could bo linked together as one Colony. All these questions and others besides, when studied properly ns to their effects, would in framing a constitution have presented as many

problems of most difficult solution, requiring time, preparation, and the mind of a fir-t-rate statesman to bring harmony among the discordant matters, if possible. But among the Danish ministers of that time, there was one gifted with the faculty, not indeed of solving difficulties by study, but of shutting his eyes to them. This minister had the supreme direction of tho colonial affairs, which then, just after the emancipation of slaves hero, were neither unimportant nor easy of settling. These affairs, on the contrary, often proved difficult and troublesome, but on such occasions, this great minister had a remedy at hand. lie pronouncod the mystic words þÿ Colonial þÿLaw, as a oh arm with which he would level down all difficulties. In your paper of lfitli inst. two principal institutions in the Danish Westindies, those of the Colonial Council and the Burgher Council, have received an attack, which is, as severe as it is, undeserved. To endeavonr to bring about a reform of sucli laws as have ceased to be beneficial to the purposes for which they were adapted or that have been found unequal to the exigencies for which they were ntended, is certainly laudable; but it is quite the opposite to aim at an overthrow ot the very institutions and laws, through which reforms are attainable, and as surely as the former is productive of good, so is the latter productive of evil. The Colonial Council is yet in its infancy and has not as yet borne the quantity of good fruit that is expected from it, hut st. II it cannot be denied, that we have already tasted the sweets of some few of its beneficial productions. It was at first and must slill he acknowledged as one of the greatest boons granted to the colonists by the mother-country, and must he looked upon as an earnest, that, in the future, we may still expect something more ; but we have yet to learn tlie full value of it: through it the mother-country at least can leant the wants of her children in her colonies, and if we raise our voices and make our wants known through the organ that is given to us for that purpose, there can he no doubt whatever, that our well founded wish sin time will be granted; we cannot have every rme tliit wo u>k for at once, and wlmt would

It is not, known that auy person in these Colonies, leaving issue, has made use of the right þÿ according to the Danish þÿCode 5-4-15 s ol disposing by will ol one half of his property for charitable purposes, and a restriction in this respect will be of little const quence as compared with the extended right of disposing of by will for tlie benefit of private individuals. Viewing the enactments in the Ordinance of 21st May 1815 paragraphs 26 and 27 w ith regard to tiic cap eial right of disposing of by will possessed by freehold proprietors and proprietors of large estates not entailed (Sicdegaarde), it might be doubtful, whether, in analogy herewith, it should not he enacted that Inhabitants of these colonies, leaving issue and making use of the right of disposing by will, aceoiding to the Rescript of 15th November 1765, of their estates in favor of one of their children, should not be entitled to dispose of one lliiid of the rest ot his property, hut only of a smaller part a- for instance one sixth or one eighth. But, the opinion has prevailed that, considering tlie peculiar circumstances of the Colonies, where there is every reason to give to the luhnbitanls us extensive a l ight of disposing of by will as possible, there is not sufficient
reason for any such restriction.

ON MATTERS AND THINGS GENERALLY, BY E. A. HEILBUTH. 1. (sAoaudi (Concluded.) This phenomenon of a fundamental law was signed by II. M. the King on the 26th March 1852. ft cannot be said that it created any profound sensation in the Colonies, either in one way or anutber, the people being stoically indifferent about it. Nor, in truth, was there much in it to carry away people's feelings ; and in spite of the pomp and parade made about it, by its sponsor Governor Feddersen, the law was everywhere met with coldness, and, as if instinctively, regarded as something not wanted. In its first paragraph, which institutes the Colonial Council with the doubtful prerogative of ooly a consultative voice in the exercise of the legislative power, the law itself commits an attempt at suicide, or points out to the Council it creates, the way of killing itself, by approving a priori of its splitting into two distinct Councils, and thus throwing an authentic doubt upon its practicability, a hint which one con poneut part of the Colonies was prompt in taking. Only, it would have been better if St. Thomas had at once pronounced for a separate Council, which, in fact, it has not even yet done, may be for tho reason that it wishes rather no Council at all. ft is certainly very questionable, whether a separate Council of this sort for each of the Islands would prove of any benefit to them. I am inclined to think, that a Council of this nature, having almost no power to do any good, can be kept from doing harm, only by giving to it a largo sphere of action, but, that, when con-

fined within narrow limits both of matter and of space, all the petty local sentiments and influences, otherwise pent up for want of such a God-send of an organ as a deliberative Council, will find their natural outlet there ; and the Council, not being able to carry any desired object in a reasonably short time, nor to strike the imagination of people either by lucid discussions, or by conspicuous results, will be led to do as much mischief as possible, for the want of doing something. I aui convinced, aud I am suro all who have reflected earnestly upon the subject will agree with me, that no Council at all of this nature, is preferable to two distinct Councils for the two Islands. I feel likewise convinced, however, that in almost every possible respect, there are such radical differences in all the relations of the two Sister-Islands, and that the inhabitants of the one know so little of the wants and interests of the other, that a joint Assembly is impracticable, and could never have been instituted, even temporarily, ii a proper study had preceded the labors of the minister and his delegate. It is obvious, that citizens of St. Thomas, being for the most part strangors and having their own important commercial business to attend to, can take no great interest in a Council, sitting in another Island and deliberating upon matters, most ot which are foreign to them and their interests, deliberating too, not with any authority to decide or to carry anything, but merely upon advice or opinions to

be given to somebody in Copenhagen, who may or may not follow such advice. It sounds like irony to speak of this as of a benefit conceded by ltoyal favor to the people of St. Thomas and St. Johns, and to ask of these people to spend their time, labor and money in corning over here to sit as members in this Council. Even for the pleasure of a trip to this Island, the thing will not take, it being rather expensive to travel forward and back and make a stay here of from 8 to 10 weeks, all at one's own expense. It is

even a wonder, that people living in this Island, can be found, willing to spend their time and' labor upon such an ungrateful task. How ill adapted this institution is to these Colonies, how impossible in its application, and of how little utility for any practical purpose, the Institution itself abundantly illustrates. It gives no constitutional government to the Colonies, and yet it abolishes the absolute government, thus creating a middle thing between the two, which common sense and experience alike have ever demonstrated to be impossible. The Council it eiects, although being merely consultative, is not left to be elected by the free choice of the inhabitants, nor even of the eduj voted is narrowed catcd part of them, but the right to vote and be by a high census, and a fifth part of the members are nominated by the Government. Its deliberations are held within closed doors, one of the members acting as Secretary, and not even a reporter or sho'rt-hand writer being permitted from without. What a member says in the Council, he may as well say at home to himself, for no one takes it down, the Secretary merely inserts in the abstracts, that Mr. N. N. took part in the discussion, which important intelligence is communicated to tho public two or three weeks after the sitting in which such an interesting discussion took place. The public being kept ignorant of what is passing in the Council, it follows, of course, that they can feel no interest therein, and that they

cannot support by their appreciation, any member who really exerts himself to promote their interests ; and the consequeuce is, t'iat members, feeling this want of support from the I public, without which their exertions are wholly in vain, find it impossible to carry any measure, which others might oppose either from interested motives, or for tho love of opposing. One of the peculiarities iu the condition of these Colonies to which I have briefly alluded, is their small number of well-educated inhabitants, and the travelling propensities of these. It is not easy to find members to vote upon, and when found and eleeted, they arc often far away from here when tho Assembly is called in. To what an extent this cause operates against the whole institution, is demonstrated iu tho plainest manner by the fact, that although the j Colonitl law ordains, that the Council is to be held every year, it has as yet been held only three times in seven years, viz., the first in 1852, the second in 1854 and tho 3rd in 1S56. It would seem, that, having been without the Council now during three years and neither missing it, nor suffering damage therefrom in any way, wc have stood the test that we entertain no violent attachment to it, and could get along well enough without it. The fact proves that the Colonial Council is not a necessary ingredient in our political life. What a vast difference between the effects caused in Denmark by the Institution of the Provincial Diets, and the effects caused here by

the Colonial Council. At home, 14 years sufficed to ripen their consultative Institution into a fully developed liberal constitution, while here, seven years have barely passed over onr Institution, and we see it decayed, unchcrished by anybody, and dying without leaving a trace of having fructified, except in a lot of tax-laws. At home, the two separate Provincial Assemblies felt and manifested from the very beginning of their existence, that strong desire of uniting in one body, which is necessary to make an Assembly powerful, and which at last becomes irresistible ; while hero, even the second Assembly wituessed the repugnance of St Thomas to send members to it. These facts are obvious, undeniable, and they clearly prove, that such an institution cannot thrive here, because, not only is it ill adapted to the condition of our Colonics but it is not wanted here. It is felt to be more of a shadow than a substance, to have no power, no influence, and to give no guarantees whatever. From its beginning few had any faith in it, and many looked upon it as only a new Government-Office. This view was strengthened when our most worthy Secretary of Government took the unhappy fancy to bo elected a member thereof, for, what with the governor as the King's Commissary, the four nominees of government, and such members as depended on government either as debtors or as functionaries, besides such others who are the parasites of government, there was already cn- I tirely too much of governmental element in the
j Council. Now, this was most unfortunate and impolitic The government and the Secretary

thereof have to frame the laws which are laid before the Council, whose deliberations upon them ought to be unbiassed and uninfluenced by the presence and the persuasions of any person connected with the government. If the Council was constituted for advising the Homegovernment, then their advice should be given, not by the governing persons, but by the governed ones, elected by their fellow-citizens, The Government can at all times give their opinions or advice, independent of the Colonial Cuuncil, and they should enable this Council to give their advice when asked for, independent of Government opinions. This must in common sense have been tbe intention in creating the Council, and had it been carried out, the Institution might perhaps now have been in a less perishing condition. But it is a natural thing, where so many depend on government, or at least desire to stand well with them, that a candidate from among Government has no chance of being rejected. Be it so ; but then, let us agree, that the Council is superfluous ; and let us try to find an Institution, that will iu a more effective and tar less troublesome manner, do for the Colonics, what this Council was intended to do ; an Institution, by which a strong and enlightened Government can, without having to descend in the lists for being elected members of an advising body, make good their legitimate influence and at the same time represent the wants and desires of the Colonies at home. As the Colonial Council can make no laws, and as

its advice is at the mercy of more powerful bodies, let there be an end to it, and let the shadow of the Colonial Legislation lest where that legislation substantially is, viz : with the King and the Danish Parliament, with the advice of 6uch a Colonial Government, as iu my next 1 shall try to delineate

The Law of the 29th December 1857 concerning the attainment of majority by f males, is hereby and in the following manner ext nded to the Danish YVestiudia Fos-essions with such modifications, as arc necessary. 1. From the ls,t July 1860 unmarried finals shall, on attaiuiug the age of 18 years, be of age under a curator, and shall, on attaining the age of 25, be of full age. 2- The payment of funds in trust of the Upperguardians on the 1st July 1860 and belonging to unmarried females wlio have filled their 18th year, shall not be demandable by them, in accordance with this present Ordinance, before the expiration of 3 years from said date ; the Upperguardians, however, being at liberty during this period to pay out such funds, when rendered feasible, by new funds being committed to their trust or by the payment of funds after legal notice ; the parties concerned however, to receive due notice 3 months previously to their funds being paid to tliem.

The Motives on which this Draft ol an Ordinance is based, are as follows: The law concerning the attainment of majority by females that emanated under date of the 29th December 1857 for Denmark, contains the following enactments : " 1. From the 1st May 1858 unmarried females shall, on attaining the age of 18 years, be of age under a curator, and shall, on attaining the age of 25 years, be of full age. 2. The payment of funds, at proscnt in trust of the Uppcrguardians, and belonging to unmarried females who have filled their 18th year, shall not be demandable before the expiration of 3 years from the date of this present law coming in force.'' Although the 1 of this law makes an entire change in the legal position hitherto occupied by females, doing away entirely with that state of minority in which unmarried females, according to the Danish Laws, hitherto have been ; and placing them with regard to the right ot disposing of their property, and with regard to contracting obligations, on the same footing as men, yet its extension has been advised by the different law-courts and by the Upperguardians here, their opinion on the question having been taken by Government. It must also be admitted that females in t Lis climate are even developed at an earlier age, than in the mothercountry, and that their greater industry and economy, as compared with that of men, shows itself even more frequently in the Colonies, than in the mother-country. In the Draft it is proposed to fix the date

for the coming in force of tiie Ordinance to the 1st July 1860 that it may be duly made known, at least 4 months before. The Government considers that a simple consequence of the law will be, that unmarried females having attained their 25th year will he able to marry without the consent of their parents, and that consequently the enactment in tlie Ordinance of the 30th April 1824 3, No. 6 will be essentially modified The 2nd of the Law enacts that the payment of funds in trust of the Upperguardians at the date of the emanation of the Law, the 29th December 1857, and belonging to unmarried females, who at that time have attained the age of 18 years, is not to be demandable by them from the Upperguardians, before the expiration of 3 years from the dato of the Law's coming in force, to wit from the 1st May 1858. Unmarried females who attained the age of 18 years during the time between the 29th December 1857 and the 1st May 1858, having on the

® II ® H X & W D contrary, being entitled, immediately after the 1st May 1858, to demand their funds in trust of the Upperguardians being paid out to tbem and their curators. Property consisting not in funds, but in real estate or moveables, can not be considered as included under this enactment and must, without doubt, have passed from the hands of the Upperguardians immediately after the law had come in force. The object of the enactment is only to postpono the payment of fuuds Lorn the Upperguardians, as otherwise, agreeable to 1 of the law, payment might be demanded as soon as the parties concerned had become of age ; but, if certain funds in trust of the Upperguardians and belonging to a girl passed the age of 18, are, agreeable to especial testamentary or other disposal, to be paid over to her, on her attaiuiug, for instance, her 21st year ot age, she must, in despite of the 2 of the Law, be entitled to demand tlie fulfilment of such disposal. If, on the contrary, funds in trust of the Upperguardians, and belonging to an unmarried female, are, agreeable to an especial disposal, cfr. the Oidinance of 21st May 1845 28, to remain in their trust during lier life time, the interest only being paid to her, tlio law will not give a right to demand the payment of such funds. The enactments of the law will not prevent the Upperguardiuns from being able to give the holders of such funds notice of payment to be demanded, even before that time, if it should be necessary to pay them out immediately after the expiration

of the 3 years. Nor is the enactment an obstacle to the Upperguardians paying out, before the lapse of the 3 years, funds belonging to an unmarried female, to her and her curator, if such payment should bu considered desirable ; the consent, however, of herself and curator being, as it would seem, necessary in this latter case, as the Law does not contain any such term for previously giving notice of such payment as is fixed for a similar case in the Law of 29th December 1857 2, enacting that minors funds Dot exceeding 100 Rd. are, in future, not to bo committed to the trust of the Upperguardians. The priucipal motive for the enactment in 2 is that a sudden notice of payment to be demanded of all funds in trust of the Upperguardiaus, at the time of the emanation of the Law, and belonging to unmarried females above the age of 18 years, must be considered as dangerous at a time when money is scarce and credit extended to its utmost. It was likewise thought that by this enactment a gradual transition would be obtained for the coming in force of the eff< cts of the law with regard to the right of disposing over their funds acquired by females, who, in consequence of the law, had been made of age ; but this last object must be considered as of minor importance, as the above shows that there is nothing to prevent the Upperguardians from paying these fuuds before the expiration of the 3 years. The Upporguardians in these islands have recommended that a similar clause as tlio one

in the 2 of the Law, should be added in tlie Ordinance for these islands. The Government is likewise of the opinion that it would not be advisable, under the depressed state of credit that, during tho latter years, has existed in these islands, to transfer to females, who in accordance with the Ordinance had become of age, their funds committed to the Upperguardians, whether these consist in bonds or bondshares, cfr. the Ordinance of the 5tli May 1830, 14, as the debtors would bo subjected to receive sudden notice to pay the bonds, either by tho original owners of such funds, or by those to whom the bonds had been transferred alter having passed out of tho hands of the Upperguardians. By fixing a period of 3 years, as in the mother-country, before the expiration of which, females who have become of age, are not to bo entitled to demand the payment of their funds in trust of the U pperguardians, a part ol the new funds committed to their charge during these 3 years will be available for gradually paying out itt the manner enacted by 13 of the Ordinance of the 5th May 1830, the funds of such females as have become of age. The debtors would hereby escape receiving notice to pay, or at all evontsget the payments postponed until the expiration of the 3 years, both, however, provtdiug that the Upperguardians did not from other reasons consider it necessary to give duo notice to pay, sooner. Such funds as may in the course of these 3 years be paid by deb-

tors to tho Upperguardians, will likewise be available for the purpose of paying to females becoming of age, the funds belonging to them. It has, however, been considered advisable to word the clause in the Oidinance fir these islands somewhat differently from the clause in the 2 of the Law, and in doing which particular allusion ought to be made, as was done in the original Draft of Law latd before the LandstlriDg, to the applying, in the above mentioned manner, new fuuds entrusted to the Upperguardians. The news from China lias had the effect of distracting public attention from the Italian question. The following relating to this treacherous outrage is from the Moniteur: þÿ According to the terms of Article 42 of the treaty signed at Tien-tsin on the 27th of June, 1858, the ratifications were to be exchanged at Pekin, and the French and English Ministers had, in consequence, left Shanghai to proceed to the capital of the Celestial Empire, after having announced their departure to the Commissioner of the Chinese Government. On arriving on the 20lh of June at the mouth of the Peiho, where they had been preceded by Admiral Hope, the commandant ot the English naval forces, they attempted in vain to open relations with the Chinese authorities. The entrance to the river had been closed by stockades. Admiral Hope and Captain Tricault, commanding the Cuchayla, were compelled to endeavour to force an entrance, when the forts of the Peiho immediately opened a fire from all their batteries, which had been repaired and mounted with guns of long rango. The Allies, not being in sufficient force, could not succeed in silencing them, in spite of the heroic bravery displayed by the English and French sailors and by their officers. After a contest of more than four hours three English gunboats had been sunk, and 478 officers and seamen, of whem 14 were French, were put hors de combat, Admiral

Hope and Commandant Tricault being both slightly wounded. Not being able to maintain an unequal combat, with forces which had only been intended as an escort to the French and English Envoys, the Allies were compelled to retire, and they returned to Shanghai on tho 9th of July. The þÿEmperor s Government and that of Her Britannic Majesty are concerting together to inflict the chasetisement and to obtain all the reparation which such a striking act of bad faith þÿdemands. The trial trip of the Great Eastern has succeeded beyond the utmost expectations of her shareholders and admirers. An explosion occured of an outer tfibo covering the lower part of the funnels or chimneys in the lower part of tho vessel. Some few lives were lost.

By the arrival of the Overland Mail we have nows from Hong Kong to the 22nd of July. Intelligence from the north was of the most disastrous nature, ourforc.es having been repulsidat the entrance of the Peiho with very severe loss. Mr. Bruce arrived off the Peiho on the 18th of June, and sought communication with the authorities on shore. No officers of rank were found, but some messages were interchanged between some petty officials and Mr. þÿBruce suits. s The tenour of these was, that the foreign Ministers would be allowed to proceed to Pekin by a passage to the northward, but that no manof-war would be allowed to enter the Peiho. They disclaimed acting under Imperial orders, stating that the forts and barriers were constructed by the country people to protect them against pirates. Failing to obtain any satisfactory intercourse, Mr. Bruce handed the matter over to Admiral Hop-, who, on the 25th of June, proceeded to force a passage. The result is given in the subjoined extracts from the North China IIeralii of the 9th and 14th of July : þÿ Her þÿMajesty þÿship s off , the Peiho, July 1. On the 25th of June, the negotiations with the Chinesc having come to nothing but a put ofl to gain time, the Admiral, with his flag flying in the Plover, followed by the gun-boats Lee, Nimrod, Cormorant, Opossum, Banterer, Starling, Forester, Kestrel, Jaitus and Haughty, proceeded to take up a position off the Peiho forts, ready to attack in case tlie Chinese should offer any resistance to clearing away the barriers. At

2 p m., the stations having been pretty well obtained (with the exception of tho Starling and Banterer which were on shore þÿ the former on the south and the latter on the north bank), the Plover and Opossum weighed ; tho latter proceeded to clear away a passage through the iron stakes which composed the first the struction. Two of these having been drawn, ob- Plover followed by the Opossum, passed through them, and also the second boom, which had been destroyed by tho Flag Captain on the previous night. On arriving at the second she attempted, together with the Opossum, to break through it, but without effect, Almost immediately a single gun was fired at her. and directly all the masks were rolled up and a tremendous fire was opened on the squadron, and the action became general. The I<ee, by signal from the Plover, passed through the stakes to the support of the Admiral. The Plover and the Opossum were, however, soon obliged to slip, the fire being too heavy for them, and, followed by the Lee, dropped clear of

T, Ci ef CD I X A\ \0 I) the stakes at 3.15. The gun-boat Plover suffered very much in killed and wounded. An officer was sent to the reserve to order up reinforcements, but the tide was too strong for the boats to attempt to pull up. The American flag officer very kindly offered to tow the boats up to a position to enable them to reach the gun-boats. At 4.30 the þÿenemy fire s was slackened considerably, orders were sent down to the reserve for Marines and Naval Brigades to prepare to land, and the Forester and the Opossum, together with the Toeywan, proceeded and towed them to the Nimrod, the place of rendezvous. At an early period of the action the Admiral had been wounded on board the Plover by a splinter in the thigh, and that vessel was almost entirely disabled. He shifted his flag to the Opossum. When there he took his station on the caboose, and thence issued his orders until a round shot cut the mainstay on which he was leaning, and caused him to fall to the deck, a height of some eight feet, breaking a rib, and severely shaking him. Af- | ter a short time he left the Opossum in the Du þÿChnyla gig, s and proceeded to the Cormorant, where he remain d At 5.45 the boats, having assembled alongside Nimrod, pushed for the shore as near the stakes as possible, and opposite to the left bastion, about GUO yards distant from it. The landing here was composed of mud about knee-deep, and the greatest difficulty was experienced in getting up the scaling ladders and bridges. The Marines and Naval Brigade,

a small portion of which had only just landed, pushed to the front under a very heavy tire from six guns in flank and in front. The fire from the walls of gingalls, rifles, and arrows was also very heavy. No check had hitherto taken place, but here a ditch, j 5 feet deep and 10 broad, occurred, and the men having no choice, plunged across, and thereby wetted their ammunition. A party of some 50 officers and men again pushed on and crossed another wet ditch, which took them within 20 yards of the wall. In the meantime Captains Shadwell and Vansittart, as also Colonel Lemon, having been wounded, the commands devolved on Commanders Commerell and Major Parke. It was now ab nt 9 þÿo clock, and darkness had set in. The position ol the landing party was most precarious; 50 otliceis and men alone remained in the first ditch, and about 150 in the second. Many had been killed and wounded, aad, with the exception of a small body 150 yards further Ii.ick. no reinforcements appeared to be offering, and the men already at the front were perfectly exhausted, and without dry ammunition or rifles fit to use. The officers in vain encouraged their men to charge to the walls, but it was ineffectual ; the m-ni were lew and d lie up, and even if they had not been they never could have carried them against the thousands that lined the walls. Under these circumstances the commanding officer dispatched an officer to the rear to ask for instructions, and the senior officer sent him back immediately with orders

lor the force to withdraw, as no reinforcements could be sent. Directly this order was received the wounded were dispatched to the rear by twos and threes, and two hours having been given them to get to the boats, the small advanced party retreated in good order from ditch to ditch, examining the ground in their retreat for any wounded that might have been overlooked. Many poor fellows, alas! in the retreat fell to rise no more, but tho wounded were saved and brought off In the meantime the boats of tho squadron under Captain VVilles employed themselves in embarking the wounded and landing party, and at o'clock, or a little after, they were all off. The gun-boats did their duty ably, and covered the landing party up to the latest moment it was prudent to fire ; and shortly after, as a testimony of their hard-fought day, the Lee and Kestrel sunk, and the Haughty just managed to keep herself afloat till the morning, when she went down, but fortunately out of range. At 3 a. m. the Cormorant, with the Admiral on board, and full of wounded, was so last aground that it was considered necessary to leave her, as she was right under the batteries, and at daylight the enemy would doubtless, concentrate their fire on her, whereas if she were temporarily abandoned, it was hoped that the enemy would cease firing on her, and the next ingot we should be able to get her | j off For the same reasons the Plover and Starling, i both immovably aground, were cleared of their crews. The morning of the 2Gth showed our squadron in sad

condition ; hardly a gun-bout but was disabled. However, during the day the carpenters of the squadron were employed patching them up temporarily, and the Starling having floated, her second master proceeded in a dingy and cut tier cable, when she drifted out of range with the ebb. Two night attempts were made i by Captain VVilles to recover the Cormorant and Plover, but without success. Thu þÿCormorant s þÿship s company having remained till 1 1 a.m. to endeavour to float her, a most terrific tire was opened upon her from batteries both north and south, and it soon become evident that she was sinking. Orders were therefore sent down to Commander VVodehouse ordering him to abandon her if he had no hopes. Her þÿship c s ompany and officers were embarked accordingly, but not before the water was up to her lower deck, and half an hour afterwards she went down head foremost. The same night fresh attempts were made at the Plover, but it was found impracticable, as she was full of wuter, and gave no hope of her being able to float. At. daylight the Kestrel, su.ik on the 25th, under the butteries, was observed drifting out, and, having been towed by the Janus into shoal water, was eventually recovered. During that day the enemy got on board the Plover, over the mud, and saved us the trouble of

destroying her by setting her on fire themselves, but not before a great portion of her stores had been recovered. The next two or three days the boats of the Cliessapeake were employed destroying the abandoned vessels as much as possible. I have no time to add more, as 1 hear a vessel is going to Shanghai. Pray let me hear from yon as soon as possible. We shall in all probability remain in the gulf till nearly the last.

A Vienna letter says: þÿ þÿ The Imperial decree which has just appeared for the regulation of the Protestant Church in Hungary, Croatia and Slavonia, has been favorably received by the liberal portion of tbe population of the capital, and will, no doubt, meet with the same reception in every part of the Austrian dominions. Henceforth the four millions of Protestants scattered throughout the empire enter upon the full and complete enjoyment of tlieir civil and political rights, just the same as the Roman Catholics, who in many localities had assumed the exclusive possession of the said rights. This beneficent decree grants the Protestant Reformed Church the free and public exercise of all its religious ceremonies New churches may be erected; the ministers will have unrestricted freedom in their preaching as well as in the administration of the sacramouts, baptisms, marriages, c)-c The publication of this decree will also produce the best effect in all the States of the Germanic Confederation, particularly in those of the North of Germany, where Austria had lost all her prestige since the conclusion of the last Concordat with Rome, followed by its rigorous execution. The publication of a decree destined to regulate iu a uniform manner, aud according to liberal principles, religious is worship gogues in Austria also expected. The Jews in the Jewish synawill also resume possession of the civil aud poli tical rights of which they have been so unjustly deprived in Austria; will cease to be excluded

from the right of possessing landed property ; and will be able to enter freely into any industrial or commercial operations, front which they have been hitherto interdicted iu most of tho provinces. In a word, Protestants, Greeks, united or non-united Jews, and indeed persons of all religious persuasions in the Austrian States, will be assimilated to Roman Catholics in tho free exercise of tlieir religion, aud in the exercise of their civil and political þÿrights.

ITALY. A letter from Milan, of the 6th, in the Nord of Brussels, þÿsays: þÿ A disgraceful scene has just, occurred at Bergamo. A number of patriots, among whom were several priests, wished to celebrate a funeral service in honour of those who had died for the cause of Italian independence. The bishop at fitst refused not only to take part in the ceremony, but to allow any of his clergy to do so. He, however, afterwards consented to officiate personally, but interdicted any addresses being delivered on the occasion one The Divine service was over, some of the party moment read an address, and the bishop immediately pronounced the excommunication of all the persons in the church. In the evening, the people assembled to the number of from 4,000 to 5,000, attacked the episcopal palace, and broke the doors, windows and furniture, and even threatened the bishop. A peasant in his rage went so far as to snatch a bayonet from the belt of a volunteer who was near him, and brandished it as though he would kill the bishop. 'I be latter remained unmoved, saying that he was ready to become a martyr, but begging that be might not be made to suffer too long. The priests ran off to call for the assistance of the National Guards and the Freuch troops in the garrison, but, for s,une reason unexplained, they did not interfere. The intendant alone weut to the spot, and succeeded in pacifying the þÿpeople.
