The law of the 30th November 1857, concerning proelamata in estates, is hereby and in tho following manner extended to the Danish Westindia Possessions, with such modifications as result from the geographical position of the islands and other circumstances. Proelamata are notices issued under the partition of estates, and calling upon creditors to come forward, under penalty of forfeiting their claims, within a certain time, and to substantiate their claims.

T« 0 MU A V l s , 1. In future three þÿmonths warning shall be given in notices calling upon creditors to come forward and substantiate their claims, as well, when issued under the partition of the estates of persons deceased, or of persons having made livery of their estate to their creditors, or of bankrupts and of other estates in which notice to credit is is to be issued þÿ if circumstances make it pmbabl that tile party concerned lias not contracted debts in any place out of the Danish or foreign Westindia islands. Should, on the contrary, this be the case, such notice must be issued with 6 þÿmouths warning. The mere fact of the party concerned having resided out of the Danish or foreign Westindia islands is, however, not in itself to authorize the use of the last named warning, if, beforo bis death, or before the event that occasions the partition ol bis estate, more than one year lias elapsed feom the time of liis leaving such place, and relinquishing his occupation there. $2. Notices that according to l may he issued with 3 in oitlis wa ning shall he published 3 times consecutively in the þÿ 8t Croix þÿAvis and the þÿ St. Thomas þÿTidende, and notices issued with C þÿmonth s warning, besidi s being published in the same manner in tho above named papers, shall likewise be published in the Berling-politieal- and advertising gazette. The warning to bo reckoned from the date of the last advertisement. 3. In consequence of these enactments the special Royal license hitherto necessary to be

obtained in several cases, before issuing notices to creditors under the partition of estates, shall in future be no longer necessary, nor shall the recording of such notices and their presentation in the Royal þÿBookkeepers Offices for annotation, hitherto required by law, be any longer requisite. The enactment in the Danish þÿCode s 5th B. 14 Ch. 29 Art. is hereby repealed. 4- Under the partition of t lie estates of persons deceased, who, on account of their general position in life, cannot be supposed to have stood in unusual relations, on account of trade, or other circumstances the issuing of notices to creditors may, without icgard to the value of the property 1 ft by the deceased, be omitted, if the heirs, or they to whom the Estate is transferri d, declare themselvi s willing to assume all lawful debts, in case of any claims being put forwaid laier. 5. The above enactments shall likewise be applicable, should a widow, to whom letters of administration have been granted, dcsiie to issue such notice to the creditors of her deceased husband, or, should heirs, who are themselves administrating the partition of an estate, desire to i.-sue a similar notice to the creditors of the person from whom they inherit. $« This Ordinance to come in force on the 1st May 18G0.

The Motives on which the above draft of an Ordinance is based, arc, as follows : Several years back it had been under consideration in the Royal Danish Chancery, when the question was mooted with regard to a change in the laws concerning the issuing of proelamata, under the partition of estates in the Westindia Islands, whether it would not be advisable, likewise, to introduce reforms in the Laws on this subject for Denmark, particularly with reject to the length of the warning to be giveu, according to the different character of the estates. The correspondence carried on at that time, between the Chancery and the Upper Court in Copenhagen, on this subject will be found in Algreen- Ussings collection of Rescripts for 1847 pages 191- 208 But after the case bad been referred to the law-adviser of the crown, and a draft of an Ordinance had been writteu þÿ the subject was postponed. As the Ministry of Justice, however, was of opinion that there was no longer any reason to postpone a final settlement of this question, it caused a new draft of a Law on this subject to be written. In this draft one of the principal clauses was to the effect, that proelamata issued

under the partition of estates were, in future, to be issued in the form of a notice to creditors, in the public papers, to come forward, before the expiration of 3 or 6 months, the latter, in case the party concerned was to be considered as likely to have contracted debts at places not in Europe, the former if the contrary should be the case; whereas the special Royal liceuse hitherto necessary to bo obtained in certain cases for issuing such notices, as well as the recording of such notices required bylaw, were to be done away with. It was originally the intention to make the law comprise the Westindia Possessions as well as Denmark, and the draft contained therefore expressly an enactment to the effect that notices to creditors under the paitiiiou of estates in tbes islands þÿ were to give 0 months warning, it the parties concerned could be supposed to have contracted debts in the mother-country it likewise being enacted that notices with 3 months warning, as well as with 6 months warning, were to be published in the Berling political- and advertising gazette, and in estates being partitioned in the Westindia Possessions, likewise in the St. Croix Avis. This draft was by the Ministry of Justice transmitted to the Ministry for the joint interior affairs of the Monarchy, requesting in a despatch of 25th May 1857 to know, whether it would be possible to obtain the opinion of the Colonial Council on tlie draft, in time to lay the same before the Diet in its Session in October of the same

year. The Ministry of Justice observed at the same time that it might possibly be advisable to retain the enactment giveu in the Placard of the 2t tU April 1814 for the Westindia Possessions, viz: that notices to creditors to couie forward within a certain time, issued in estates of persons deceased and in which the amount of means did not amount to more than 400 Rd. W. C. need only be published in the St. Croix Avis, and be presented for annotation in the Royal þÿBookkeepers Offices iu these Islands, in which ease it would be necessary to add an especial clause to that effect to the Liw. The above quoted earlier discussions on the subject (cfr. Algreen- Ussings collection of Rescripts for the year 1847 page 194, and pages 206 þÿ 207) show that the question was raised as to whether there was sufficient reason to retain the rule existing then in Denmark with regard to irotices to creditors issued in cases, in which there was a presumption that there existed creditors in the Westindies, namely, that such notice was likewise to be recorded iu the Up percourt in the W?stindia Possessions, published in the St. Croix Avis, and presented in the Royal þÿBookkeepers Offices for annotation, or if it would not bo more proper to repeal this rule on account of the trouble and expense connected with it, and instead thereof to adopt the official measure of making all such notices, as were published in the Berling paper with the longest warning, known in the papers in these islands, without any cost, however, to the

respective estates, auJ without an omission in this respect exercising any influence on the validity of the notice issued to Creditors of the estate. Accordiug to the abovementioned communication from the Ministry of Justice to the Ministry for the joint iuterior affairs of the Monarchy, the previous draft contained a clause for cases in which circumstances led to the presumption, that a person, whose estate was being partitioned in Denmark, had contracted debts in tire Westindia þÿI esse.-sions, in case ot which, an especial notice to creditors, besides the general one, should be given 3 times consecutively in the St. Croix Avis, and that a period of 3 months from the date of' the last publication in the paper should expire, beforo the property of the estate was partitioned. But the Ministry of Justice did not deem it necessary that any such especial rule should be given for such cases, as, if 6 months warning was considered sufficient for the most distant parts of the world, it must likewise be considered so for the Westindia Possessions, at the same time that, according to the relations existing between the mother country and the Colonies, it might generally be presumed that existing debts were on the side of the Colonies. To carry out still more effectually the measures approved of in Our most gracious Rescript of the 4th April 1849, and by which the Westindia dollar (1 dollarto 1(H) cents) was introduced into the Danish Westindia possessions as legal tender, small coin of the following kind shall be coined lor circulation there, viz.: 20, 10 5 and 3 kcent-pieces, all of silver, and 1 cent-pieces of bronze.

I have endeavored to prove, both theoretically and by facts, that the Colonial Council is ill adapted to tbe Colonies, as being rather cumbersome than uselul, and being on the whole not wauted in the Colonies. This is in a great measure owing to the absence of authority and power in the Council ; but 1 make bold to say, that, according to the best of my conviction, even a Constitution granting all constitutional attributes and powers, would have uo better chance of success, aud for the same reason, the peculiar conditions of these Colonies, which render a constitutional colonial Government impossible, aud among these conditions, principally the one, that the Colonies and the Government and the Legislation are Danish, but their populatiou foreign. Having characterised the Colonial Council as useless aud cumbersome, I shall, iu order to silence the few blind adherents, whioh it is the fate of all Government-measures to have, make good my accusation by illustrating how the said Council works, and to what a degree it complicates and impedes the machinery of Government. Suppose then a certain measure, a law or an alteration in an existing law, involving perhaps an outlay of some money, or a diminution iu some public revenue, in short, a measure of may be no great importance in itself, but aiming at a highly desirable object, to be felt necessary, then tbe Government will frame a draft of an

ordinance, sometimes, I believe, after first having corresponded with the Ministry about it this draft will thereafter be submitted to the law-officers in the Colonies, whose opinions thereon may differ, and cause alterations to be made in the þÿdraft it will next be laid before the Colonial Council for advice, and then, no matter what this advice, sent to Copenhagen to bo either assented to, or altered, rejected by or tho Ministry, according as the circumstances may þÿbe, aud, if not rejected by tho Ministry, to be brought before the two Houses of the Danish Diet, and ther- go through the same

process as at the þÿMinistry s, and lastly, before the King. And this is the shortest wav any law has to travel before it can come in force here. But now let us fancy, that the measure in question may concern some Communal interest, then, the law-draft must be submitted also to the three Burgher Councils of tho Islands ; and next, it would be very curious to reflect upon, þÿ what would bo the result, i if, iustcad of one Colonial Council, there were two, each of them giving their advice, aud not unlikely, a diametrically opposite advice each to the other. It can hardly be imagined of frequent oci urrence that all the said bodies, viz : the Colonial Government, Law-Officers, Burgher Councils, Colonial Council or Councils, Minister, the Danish Parliament and the þÿKing s Government will which arrived at that colony in the ship þÿl ln- agree upon any measure ; as it is, the advice of the Colonial Couucil has as yet seldom proved fate to possess the greatest share in of a 1 iw-draft. If there is any truth in the determining the proverb: þÿ many cooks, þÿ&e. then we should get little good out of our law-pot, and I think Dickens would have felt somewhat ashamed at his paltry Circumlocution-Office, had he known our array of such Offices. Now, I suppose, I may be held blameless for calling the Colonial Council cumbersome and a nuisance in the way of a vigorous Government. I have now arrived at tbe grave task which for one of the first and most important proposed in the prelude to these disquisitions, I of the

subjects to be discussed, namely to suggest an Institution to replace the Colonial Council. If this Council is and will ever bo a failure, and if a thoroughly constitutional Government must be acknowledged to be impossible here, wbat then, is there, that the Colonies may waDt in their stead? I here is, what I have already several times named: a vigorous Govcrnuiciil. This moaDs not an arbitrary Government, nor indeed a military one, not a Governor at whose frowns people tremble; it means a Government strong in ability and knowledge, strong from being composed of the ablest men to be had, strong from being known fo he just and impartial and a true mouth piece of the Colonies ; it means a Government with sufficient power and faculty to act on its own responsibility, without having first to submit almost every measure to the Ministry, and without being trammeled by a Bureau of Decision. department of Revision, or censured by a It means, in short, a Government to reside in the Colonies, not only in name, but in reality, not as to the persons only, but as to the power also. And, as the former Council, called the þÿ Royal Westindia Governabolished to make room for a Guvernor temerity, þÿment was, with au incomprehensive with thj Colonial Council, so will it be necessary to reinstitute that Council on the cessation of the Colonial Council. In plain words, the only satisfactory solution, which upon much reflection I have been able to find, and wherein nearly every thinking persou iu these Colonies agrees

with me, is substantially the former Wertindia Government, minus tbe arbitrary power, vested iu a Governor-General, and plus, a more ample power for the Council, besides the full liberty of the Press under the Danish Picss-Law of April 3d, 1851 As every body knows, the Government in the Colony is at preseDt vested in one pcrsoD, who exeieises it under the Colonial Director under the Minister of Finance in Copenhagen It is quite natural, that no very extensive powers should be entrusted to the exercise of only one person, and it is just as natural, that this person, as the sole depository of the power and responsibility of Government, will, iu common prudence, decline to be entrusted with a very extensive power, or, at all events, to exercise it. Hint ilia lachrymal ! For as long as the Colony is at a distance of 5,000 miles from the Homo-Government, and at least until this distance is annihilated by electricity, the Colony requires its Government with its power to reside within it. This culls for no elucidation, it is demanded by common sense, and its necessity is proved by ten years experience here. The Governor has at present only two sources to seek advice at, (the Colonial Council being left out of contemplation j the odo of them dangerous, tho other irresponsible. By the first I allude to tho Chief Justice of tbo Colony, the Governor being directed to take his advice when required, and this I call dangerous, because, iD my opinion, as in that of all jurisconsults, a judge should be judge only,
and least of all, Government-adviser ; by tbe second, I mean tbe Government-Secretary, who is not a member of Government, aud has no

other authority than what the Governor may delegate to him, and who is responsible only for the expediting the Acts of the Governor, and for carrying out his orders. This state of things affords very little guarantee for its woiking well ; but while it is susceptible of much improvement, it actually points out as it were, that this improvement is to be found in a responsible Council, a Council of Government appointed by the King, participating in the exercise ol Government and bearing their share of its responsibility. I Such a Council is indispensable, and, in justice i to the Governor, as in justice to the Governed, it ought at once to be instituted. With it the Colonies may have a strong Government, its members dividing the business among them, and expediting it in a reasonable space of time ; the Clnef- Justice will then be left, as be should be, entirely to bis judicial functions ; and there will be no thriving for outside councillors and advising busy-bodies. Then every measure could hope to be regarded with impartiality, and to be fairly discussed so as to be placed in its real true light, and on its own merits, for nothiug is truer than the Fiencli saying : de la discussion nait la lumicre ; but, as it is now, discussion is unlortunately discarded. It will probably be argued agaiust me, that in some Colonics, particularly iu the British WVstindia Colonies, there is only a Governor with a Secretary ; this, at least, I have often heard in defence of this measure having been introduced

here. But it is totally fallacious. In every one of the British Colouies there is a constitutional Assembly, aud in most of them, a Couucil besides, tunning the Upper House iu the Assembly, then, each Colony has its Attorney-Geueral and Solicitor General. The Spanish Colonies have each a Royal Audiencia or Government Council, and an lutendancia independent of the Captain Geueral, and lastly in each of the French Colouies there is a Council acting with the Governor, besides a Procureur Imperial The Danish Colonic s, when their Colonial Council has failed to fulfil its aim, staud iu this respect alone. But, it will he further argued against me from my own words in the beginning of my first Article, that the same Government cannot at the same time be constitutional in Denmark and absolutist here. This maxime I certainly entertain, though I see it pruductivc of the greatest difficulties in solving it in a manner beneficial to the Colonies It is, however, capable of being solved, and it presents to my mind several modes of solution, none of them very perfect, certainly, but, at least, more or less practicable. 1 shall further on return to this very difficult and very interesting question. M anwhile, I give as the result of my disser- i tation on the Administration of the Colonies: that the local Administration should he vested in a Governor and two Councillors , as the Royal W'estinilia Government , and under it a President for i St. Thomas and St. Johns, all of them to be

of course civil functionaries possessed of legal knowledge. That the Chief of the Military Force in the Colonies be placed under the orders of the Governor ; that the Revision and Decision of accounts shall be done in the Colony , or shall at all events regard only the Accountants and not touch the Governmeul ; that the Danish Press Law of 3d April 1851 be extended to the Colonies ; and that this Royal Westindia Government be collectively invested with vice-regal authority. To be continued.

The Ministry for the joint interior affairs of the monarchy expressed in its answer to the Ministry of Justice, that it was d sirnble that the law should comprise the Wcstindi i P ssessions, as well as Denmark, but concurred, at the same time in the opinion, that it was necessary to give to the authorities in the Colonies, principally the Colonial Council, an opportunity to give its opinion on such clauses of the draft, as were peculiar to the Colonies, it being also desirable, that their opinion should be heard with regard to clauses that will exercise an indirect influence in the Colonies. There was however not sufficient time to obtain the opinion from the different Authorities in the Westindies before the session of the Diet in October 1857, and as the Ministry of Justice did not consider it advisable to postpone laying a draft of such a law before the Diet, this was done, omitting the especial enactments for the Westindi.i Possessions, as will be seen from the draft communicated in the þÿ Department Tiþÿdende for 1857 pages 865 to 870. After the subject had been discussed in the Diet, the law of the 30th November 1857, concerning pnoclamata to be issued iu estates, emanated, and is as follows : 1. In future three months warning shall be given in notices calling upon creditors to come forward and substantiate their claims, as well, when issued under the partition of the estates of persons deceased or of persons having made livery of their estate to their creditors, or of bankrupts, and of

other estates in which notice to creditors is to be issued þÿ if circumstances make it probable that the party concerned lias not contracted debts in any place out of Europe, or in Iceland and in the Fat6 Islands. Should, on the contrary, this be tho case, such notice must be issued with 6 months warning. The mere fact of the party concerned having resided out of Europe or in Iceland, or in the Faroe Islands is, however, uot in itself to authorize the use of tho last named warning, if, before his death, or before the event that occasions the partition of his estate, more than one year lias elapsed from the time of his leaving such place, and relinquishing his occupation there. 2. The notice to creditors treated of in 1 shall be published three times consecutively in the Berling- political- and advertising gazette, and, when not in the civil diocese of Zealand, likewise in the official gazettes of the respective civil dioceses, and when in the Island of Bornholm, in such newspaper, as may be selected by Government. The warning to be reckoned from the date i of the last advertisement. 3. In consequence of these enactments, the special Royal license hitherto necessary to be obtained in several cases before issuing notices to creditors under the partition of estates, shall, in future, be no longer necessary, nor shall the recording of such notices, hitherto required by law, be any longer requisite. The especial enactments for Bornholm concerning the forms under which notices are to be issued

there, warranted by the Royal Resolution of 29th August 1832, made known by the Placard of the 11th September of the same year, shall likewise cease to bo in force. The enactment in the Danish Code's 5th B. 14th Ch. 29th Art. is hereby repealed. 4 and 5 are the same as the 4 and 5 of the Draft of the Ordinance. 6. This law is not applicable to the Faroe Islands. CHRISTIANSTED, ST CROIX TUESDAY, 22nd NOVEMBER, 1859. þÿ The Colonial Council was convened on Saturday last in all the grandeur of secrecy. No profane feet were permitted to cross the threshold of the room now devoted to the labors of this august assembly. Except on the ground of amne ignolum pro magnijico, we cannot but thiuk, that this secrecy is totally subversive of that interest which might, otherwise, be taken in the deliberations of the Council. This was acknowledged by the Council itself in the last Stssion; and au advice was forwarded, by it, to the Home Government, recommending the Meetings of the Council to be held publicly. Rut good advice, as it is proverbially said, is seldom taken and followed ; and this one has met the common fat.o The labours of our legislative advisers have, nevertheless, commenced : hut where, when, and how they will end, tio mortal can say. To judge from the measures passed during tin; last Session, in 1856, of which we have not since heard, a long while may elapse before the mighty thoughts of honourable mi tubers can ripen into acts. We await, with patience, the publicaiioii of the debates.
The European Mails arrived here yesterday. We have made extracts from the London Papers of such items of news as are most iutoiesting.
Wo read in the Copenhagen Papers, that on the 24th ult, His Majesty was pleased to appoint Mr. J. Knutiisen, formerly acting Controller, as Broker in this town.

From the St. Thomas Times, November 16. The It M. steamship Prince arrived here on Sunday morning last from Anegada, and is her final trip to the ill fated Paramatta. The officers, engineers, and operatives that remained by the latter vessel to the end have also returned here, and will proceed with the Shannon to Europe. The Paramatta is said to be split in two, lengthwise, making it dangerous for the operatives to attempt to save anything more from

her. We believe there is, nevertheless, a great many pieces of her machinery that have been saved, and are now being taken home by the Shannon. The loss which the Paramatta alone entails, would have been sufficient to have built a score of lighthouses as a warning to keep clear of those reefs on which she now lies. There is now, however, a prospect that the Governments of the United States and Great Britain, and such other as may sec the desirability of a lighthouse there, wiil unite in erecting one.

COMMUNICATION. To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Dear Sir, Seven days have passed since the Colonial Council was convened, and yet the public 1ms not been blessed with a sight, in your paper, of any of its proceedings. It cannot be that the members of that assembly are so indifferent to the opinion of their constituents, as not to desire to stand well with them. And vet it would appear so; since, no oue of them c,r s to interest himself so far as to look af or th publication of the debates. Can you throw any light on the subject ? Nov. 22, 1859. One who watches w ith interest the doing) of the Colonial Council.

CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX. FRIDAY, 25th NOVEMBER, 1S59 þÿ þÿ þÿ One who w itches with interest the doings ol We are unable to reply to the question of the Colonial þÿCouncil, further than to state, that we have not received a line from the Colonial Council for publication. We regret this tlio more, as our establishment being, as is to be expected, small, we are unable to execute work with any great dispatch. This we might, nevertheless, be called upon to do, should the publication of the debates be delayed until more printing-work accumulates than we can execute in a short time We would I e wanting, however, in the exercise of economy an i in the regard for self interest, did we enlarge our establishment without feeling a demand for it. The purchase of muteiials would lie but a secondary consideration, compared to the possi- in bility of obtaining workmen. No printer, these islands, would accept of any employ m tit but a permanent one ; and it would be something not very short of nmdness, to keep six or more men constantly in our employ, when wo can only find woik for two during thirty months in the space of three years Even supposing the Colonial Council did meet yearly, we could still not pay wages to a large number of woik men during the whole year, only to enable us to execute the Colonial þÿCouncil swork whenever that body should he convened. Wo are happy in having obtained this opportunity to set ourselves right in the eyes of the public, as the Colonial Council, in its last Session, was pleased to report to His Majes-

ty the King, that "on account of the deficient condition of the local press the publications on the diverse matters discussed in general only appear long after closed " To avoid this very far-stretched cause they are despatched and the sessions of complaint, we think the Council might he more expeditious in sending to us its proceedings and not allow more work to accumulate than we can hurriedly execute.

Muzzini Inis subscribed 200C to the Garibaldi fund for purchasing a million of muskets ; his subscription was accompanied by the following letter: þÿ scud þÿ I 2001'. as my contiibution to General þÿGaribaldi sfund, to which 1 feel sure that all who share my political faith will hasten to subscribe. The name of Garibaldi is a guarantee that these arms will not he employed merely in the delence of Cattolica and the Mincio. The sacred unity of our country, violated by every idea which does not embrace tlio whole of Italy, from the heights of the Tyrol to the Sicilian Sea, is an article of faith for him os well as for us These arms, then, are to be used for us. ROMAN STATES The Pope returned to Rome on the morning of the 20 h inst. A great crowd was assembled on his passage through the city. The interview between the Pope and the King of Naples has been adjourned. The Pope has dispatched an English prelate, named Talbot, to the Court of Naples, in order to explain, the cause of the adjournment of the interview. Conferences have been held between the Pope and the Due do Grammout, on the subject of which complete secrecy was observed; but it is stated that the ordonnanecs for granting administrative reforms are now ready, and will shortly be made public. The Government has received intelligence that the Bishop of Rimini and other priests had been imprisoned, and that the authorities at Pesaro had seized letters from emissaries exciting to rebellion the provinces now held in submission by the Papal troops. Many priests have quitted the country in the neighbourhood of the Romagna on accouut of the intrigues ol emissaries, and in fear of disturbances.

NAPLES. Garibaldi has sent forth his summons to the Neapolitans in the following þÿProclamation : þÿ þÿ To our Brothers of Naples ! þÿ Brothers ! we have combated the Austrians ; we have fought these insolent oppressors of Italy, and we have beaten them. We have seen them run like rabbits before our young soldiers; we have seen them id v in terror, and beg their lives of those whose brothers, parents and friends they had like cowards before the suns of those basely assassinated We have seen whom them fly they barbarously scourged or butchered at their pleasure ; we have seen them fly, the vile miscreants, before the comrades of Ugo Bassi, Civeaghi, Ciceruacehio, and ask their lives with a baseness unmistakeably Austrian ; and yet of those who surrendered or who were wounded the Italians did not kill a single one. Brothers! we have fought as Italians fight when they are united, and you were not with us. In the ranks

provinces, but of Naples there were few The shout of victory was hoard in every dialect except yours, and yet þÿ we knew it þÿ your hearts beat high in the cause of the country. You felt our dangers and fatigues, and your hearts exulted at the announcement of our victories. Yes, exulted iu spite of the abominable tyranny which crushes and degrades you ; it felt its overthrow by the victory of Italians. You were not with us in the body, but your good will was there, wo arc certain ; but this time, at least, you will be with us in both. Yes ; Providence has decreed the union and alliance of our family þÿ of this poor Italian family Foreigners, doctrinaires , and priests labour in vain. In vain they seek to sow discord, to excite mistrust in the public mind, to corrupt this hapless piople, whom they have divided so ofien, and so olten sold to the stranger. In vain our brothers of the south have clasped the hands of our brothers of the centre and of the north ; the sons of the Procidas, the Masaniellos, the Pepes have grasped the victorious right hand of tho soldiers of Paleslro and San Martino. þÿ Rimini, October, þÿ18.'>t>. þÿ G. The China Expedition þÿ Tho greatest indecision, we are given to understand on the v, ry best authority, at present prevails as to the course to be pursued with regard to China. Within the last week an older has been issued by the authorities at the War Office, cancelling all previous orders given for the immediate shipment of military stores for service of the expeditionary force to that country ; while, on the other hand, instructions have been received at J þÿ the Royal Arsenal, Woolwich, for the immediate preparation of a quantily of linen bandages to be sent out to China. Again, several members of the staff, who were under orders to sail on the 4th proximo, have, it is said, received countermanding orders, while the Secretary of State for War has issued a circular memorandum to the effect that distinctive marks must be put on each package to enable the military storekeeper at Hong Kong to classify, immediately on their receipt, the different stores, thereby preventing any confusion in the subsequent issues whenever required A great deal will depend on the nature of the news that will be

must be, in the long run, their master, to uphold them in the authority they may þÿ legitimately claim, the affair would be easily settled. If tho Emperor of Austria understood his own interest, or had a statesman of intellect enough to make say, him comprehend it, he would fling to þÿ þÿ the þÿwinds, his resentment against þÿwe ll Sar-

dinia, and make it his own act and deed to form such a North Italian nationality, such an Italian nationality altogether if good fortune should speed such justice, as for the Austrian empire would seal that portion of ever against wautoti or ambitious aggression from France. It is far more worth than the cession of Vcnetia to replace the old battle-ground on the map with a kingdom which for its own sake will keep the peace between France and Austria on that side, and which neither party would dare wantonly to offend. Austria may checkmate its most dangerous foe by giving more than he requires. Autriau statesmen might then indeed devote their energies to the coneiliatiou of the peoples reduc- Empire, and might by an immense of the tion of the army hope to lay the foundation of content in the alleviation of taxation. The personal pride of the Hapsburg dynasty is the only barrier to this enormous good for all parties ; and is it to be wondered at that peoonly ples, finding their rulers and their families and causes of their bitterest misfortunes the oppressions, should seek to relieve themselves of authority which is nothing but a curse, and which daily increasing intelligence will only the more clearly demonstrate to be so ( What do Hungary and Bohemia and the Tyroll owe to Francis Joseph, or any of his race, that should induce them fondly to remain his instruments for wreaking his malice on others to their own irremediable ruin ? There needs no political prescience of any but the least arnbi

tious class to see tho upshot of the present selfishness of the Hapsburg rule. It proclaims its own doom within and without. nn?*»«>- England appears to be accused in Paris of a desire to þÿ lay a þÿtrap for France in this busi ness ; and the French Government, it is said, must do its best to baulk the plan. England is simply accepting that termination of the Ita lian war which Napoleon was at so much pains to impress upon the world as being his aim. þÿ the complete enfranchisement of þÿItaly. Is it unfriendly, or cynical, or crafty, to take a man at his word ? to help him to achieve altogether what he acknowledges he has reluctantly left half completed ? The dream of an Ita lian federation, with the Pope at the head of it, is proved, by the open decision of the popula tious of , which it is to be composed, to be an idle impossibility. The introduction of Austria into this vision as voting for Venetia only the more outrageously violates the credible. An Italian monarchy is this federation in a far better shape ; it is a mechanism that will work ; it would be too much to avow that what was really required was a pretence which would not. News reaches us that is likely to cut this Gordian knot, happily or fatally as it may be Garibaldi has issued a proclamation to the Nea politans. If there be in Naples tho stuff that makes a people, he will receive an answor that will take the Italian question out of all jurisdiction but that which has the innate right to determine it. if there are the elements of a

great nation will arise ; if not, vrt may the more resignedly, if not the more happily, submit to the miserable dicta of half-hearted expediencies. Than the condition of the Neapolitan Government nothing can be more favourable to tho glorious cause. That rule has left no motive to any sane man to desire anything short of its utter destruction. Like the other Italian despotisms, it has left the certainty that nothing can bo worse, that it never can be remembered with one regret unless for tho tardiness of its fate. If there be a standard round which all Italy will nnd ought to rally, it is that of the hero Garibaldi. Let us see whether the Italians are worthy of such a leader. They are henceforth their own fate, and their next act proclaims it.

TLo splendid vessel, the Royal Charter, was totally lost on Wednesday, in Moelfre Bay, on the north-east coast of the Isle ot Aoglesea. It was supposed she had about half a million of gold on board. So destructive had been the storm along the coast on Wednesday, that the Chester and Birkenhead Railway had been de stroyed in two places ; between Conwoy and Holyhead an embankment had been washed away, and near lthyl, about a dozen yards of the line had been completely washed away, and 100 yards damaged, the passengers having to walk in the first case two miles, and in the last half a mile to get to the train on either side of the disruption. At þÿI anmaenmuwr 2J dead bodies were washed ashore during Wednesday. The following letter, dated Thursday evening, is from a correspondent at Moelfre Bay : þÿ It is my very painful duty to record the total wreck of the screw steam-ship Royal Chatter, Captain Taylor, which took place at from 0 to 8 þÿo clock on the morning of Wednesday at Moelfre, a rugged portion of the Auglesea Coast, and about midway between Amlwch and and Puffin Island. The ill-fated vessel sailed from Melbourne on the 2Gtli of August, having on board 388 passengers, of whom (i3 occupied the saloon, and a crew, including officers, of 112 persons. While the ship was passing Queenstown, on Monday morning, 13 of the passengers landed in a pilot boat. On Tuesday morning, at 11 þÿo clock, the Royal Charter spoke the steam-tug United Kingdom, which, instead of returning to port with riggers who

had been assisting in the working of a ship to Cardiff, transferred 11 of the riggers to the Royal Charter, Captain Taylor having kindly agreed to take them to Liverpool ; so that there were on board at the time of the wreck 498 souls, and of these only 39 were saved. The loss of life on this sad occasion was 459 persons. The Royal Charter had on board a large nmount of specie on freight, the exact amount, of which cannot be ascertained, as all the þÿship p s apers have been lost, hut it was variously estimated by the surviving passengers and crew at from £600,000 to <£800,000. One of the saloon passengeis, who was drowned, was stated to have had in his possession gold to the value of £10,000. The ship had only a moderate cargo, principally of wool and skins. From the time of leaving Port Phillip Heads till the art ival off the Irish coast the passage was in the highest degree favourable; she was only once in danger and then from an iceberg. After passing Quecustown the wind veered round to K.N.K., blowing strong. On Tucsdag night it blew a gale, aud continued to increase in violence, till at leugth, on the morning of the fatal disaster, it blew a perfect hurricane. Arriving off Point Lynas at 6 p.m ou Tuesday evening signal rockets were for several hours thrown up, in the hope of attracting a pilot, but none made their appearance. Captain Taylor, finding that his vessel was making ler way, aud gradually drifting towards the shoie, let go both the anchors, but such was the violei ce of the

wind and the heavy cross sea prevailing, that the chains parted. Notwithstanding that the engines were worked at their full power, the captain was unable to work to windward, and the unfortunate vessel struck the recks stern first in four fathoms water. Up to this period (about 3am) not the slightest alarm was evinced among the passengers, a large portion of whom were women and children ; the most pcifoct discipline and order prevailed. The masts and rigging were cut adrift, but caused no relief, as the ship continued to thump on the sharp pointed rooks with fearful rapidity. Shortly after she struck she was thrown broadside on, perfectly upright upon the shelving stony beach, the head and stern lying due east and west, the former not being more than twenty yards from a projecting rock. At this juncture one of the crew, a Portuguese, named Joseph Hogets, nobly voluntered to struggle through the heavy surf and convey a rope on shore. Though it was not believed by any one that danger was imminent, the captain gave the order, and Rogers ably fulfilled his duty. ChRISTIAUSTED, ST. CROIX. FRIDAY, 2nd DECEMBER, 1S-59. We have, within the last, few days, had an illustration of tlie practical working of the Colonial Council. It will he recollected, that we published some remarks on the 2 1st October, repudiating the right of the Colonial Council to recommend u measure affecting our private interests. We allude to the clause in the law-draft concerning the annulling of lost bonds, according to which, wc are to accept only a hall ot the usual payment for the publication of a summons relating to a lost bond ol a less amount than $300. The Colonial Council j being held in secret, leaves us no opportunity to know anything of its proceedings, beyond what may he gathered from an extract published in this paper. From that extract we could not perceive whether the draft, to which we allude, was under discussion or not. Nevertheless, we prepared our protest, and, in accordance with the dictates of the Colonial-Law, we endeavoured to get a member to adopt it as his own. The island in question called San Juan, which has been taken possession of by Capt. Picket and a score or two of American Soldiers, under the direction of Getil. Harney, the Officer in Command of the United States Army in Oregon, is described as about 15 miles in length and 7 broad, and of much greater importance to the British, from its proximity to the rising Colony of Victoria, and its command of the Channel, or Sound, which runs for several hundred miles between Vancouver and the mainland, than its possession can be to the State of Oregon. The Governor ol Vancouver, Mr. Douglas, has protested against the act ol Gt til. Harney, aud has iufornied the Legislatuie that ho intends to land a Company of Sappers and

The persistent mitux oi tne Chinese peasantry iu in© United States is a fact which presses itself upon the attention alike of the political econi mist, and the statesman. Throe thousand Ceh stia s are stated to be at this moment on their way to San Francisco. California already has large Chinese population. Notwithstanding their characteristic vices, the Chinamen, although not popular, are found to be useful members of society. They peiform, with alacrity and intelligence, the ruder kiudsof labour, are marvellously frugal in their habits, aud are consequently enabled to work for very low wages. Indeed, it is not improbable that the poorer inhabitants of that vast empire, wdiicli contains within its limits nearly a moiety of the human race, may bo destined to work great changes in the industrial if not in the social and political condition of Am. rica. The most obvious immediate effect of Chinese immigration, for instance, in its tendency to supplant the negro. The Coolie in California lias already made the African impossible. There, as in the West India Islands, the Malay labourer is found to be, in all respects, preferable to his darker cousin. The voluntary immigration from Canton and Shanghae into our Pacific Stutes bids fair soon to be enormous. Hitherto it has mainly been directed to California, but it will j manifestly soon extend to Oregon also. Nor is there reason to doubt that it will soon reach the Atlantic States as well. Assuming that these

natives of China may one day become as numerous among us as those of Europe, what shall their social and political status be ? Are they to be regarded as whites, or as people of colour ? Shall they, equally with immigrants from Ireland aDd Germany, be admitted to the benefits of our naturalisation laws ? These arc questions which flit and flicker now along the political horizon. But the march of events with ns is rapid, and all signs conspire to prove that we have seen only the beginning of that profouud strife of races and of principles by which the institutions of the United States are before long to be tried in the fire. þÿ New York Tim.
